Opening Scripture Reading (Romans)
Dave begins with a reading from Romans 3:25-26: “When he held back and did not punish those who sinned in times past, for he was looking ahead and including them in what he would do in this present time. God did this to demonstrate his righteousness, for he himself is fair and just. I love that. And he makes sinners right in his sight when they believe in Jesus.” The congregation responds: “This is the word of the Lord… Thanks be to God.”
He introduces the series: “We are in a series called Long Live the King… as I invite Dave to teach… great slides… download via app for your personal journey with Jesus.” Mentions David and David Shell as “best tapers.”
Detailed Vignette: First Dates with Wife Robin (Tying into Blood Theme)
Dave dives into a personal story: “On our very first dates with my wife… she fainted (painted). Perhaps because she was in the presence… We, she fainted there on the magazine aisle of an Albertsons.” Audience thinks: “What were you doing in the magazine aisle on your first date?” Dave: “I don’t like your tone. I will get there.”
Actual first date planned for Saturday: Robin won concert tickets (Alice 97.3, caller #9) to Alice in Chains Zenfest at Golden Gate Park—featuring Macy Gray, Melissa Etheridge, Alanis Morissette, Barenaked Ladies (clarifies: “band name… don’t need Jay emailing”). Robin couldn’t go, asked Dave.
Impatient, Dave asks for Friday: “Ran errands… Kragen for clutch fluid because my master cylinder was failing. Very romantic. Another errand, Albertsons… she got lightheaded and fainted because that day we had both given blood.”
Stickers: His—“I donated blood, save a life.” Hers—“Kiss me, I gave blood. I think she chose that. Nobody can see me later. Hello! We’re married now!”
Context: First date Sept 14, 2001 (3 days post-9/11). Largest US blood drive: 500,000+ units. At his school (teacher then), gym blood drive—18+ students, many forged waivers for national solidarity amid grief/helplessness. Sticker: “Donate blood, save a life.”
Transition: “I want to talk today about blood… a weird topic… I’m squeamish… reframe blood as life.”
Blood as Life: Biological Explanation
“Blood carries oxygen to cells (without it, suffocate/die), nutrients (starve without), closes toxins/heals (platelets, white cells), cycles waste (kidneys/liver/lungs). Blood is life.”
Biblical Affirmation and Theme Introduction
Bible: Leviticus 17:11—“life of a creature is in the blood” (ancient understanding matched ours). “Lose blood = lose life.”
God of life: Genesis 3—garden, tree of life. Humans choose independence, reject life → death. “Sin not inconvenient mistake… strongest terms: death. Drains life, breaks relationship w/ God (source of life).”
Romans 6:23—“wages of sin is death.” Affects all: self, others, God. Jesus: John 10:10—“life abundant.” Enemy: steal/kill/destroy.
Series Context: Why Jesus Died (Beyond Simplistic “For My Sins”)
“Long Live the King” (7 weeks, 6 to Easter): Why Jesus died, practical depth. Not just personal sins—humanity’s. Last week (Jay): Exodus Passover Lamb → Jesus as second Lamb, defeats sin/death (rescues from slavery).
Today: Another image from Exodus end/Leviticus.
The Problem: End of Exodus (Exodus 40:34-35)
God rescues (Red Sea), dwells via Tabernacle (central tent). But: “Cloud covered Tent of Meeting… glory of the Lord filled Tabernacle. Moses could not enter.” “Bad news… If Moses can’t, who can? Sin separates… God radioactive-holy.”
Goal: God w/ people (“I will be your God, you my people”)—but how?
Leviticus Solution: The Five Offerings
Leviticus opening chapters: How to approach God.

Burn offering: Burn whole animal—“I’m entirely yours.”
Grain/gift: “You’re provider… portion back.”
Peace: Kill animal, eat together—“barbecue… share meal. Delicious. Favorite.”
Sin: Unintentional wrongs (“Oh man, didn’t realize”).
Guilt (focus): Intentional—knowing wrong (justice/hurting others, disobey God). Leviticus 6: “Sins unfaithful to Lord… restitution… guilt offering: ram w/o defect… forgiven.”

Vignette: Rotten Fruit/Sin Spread
Sin like mold/rot spreading through Tabernacle/camp: “Bunch of fruit, bottom one rotten, rots upward—so gross.”
Tabernacle image (Bible Project): Altar outside Tent (priests as “butchers”), lay hands on animal (ID as substitute), kill, sprinkle blood (life/cleansing) inside/backwards thru camp—purifies community.
Vignette: Friend Ruth (prepping, speaking Saratoga): “System like mirror—shocks: sin serious (brings death), can’t pay ourselves, life must substitute.”
NT Connection: Jesus Fulfills (Romans 3:25; Hebrews 9:11-12)
Jesus: Passover Lamb + Blood Sacrifice. Rom 3:25—“presented Jesus sacrifice… shedding blood… fair, held back past sins.”
Heb 9: “Christ high priest… own blood (not goats/calves)… most holy place once-for-all, redemption forever.”
Blood shorthand: life/sacrifice. Communion: “Blood of Jesus” (juice symbolizes). Cross real (Roman, suffering)—God gives own blood (vs. pagan “appease gods”).
Practical Implications: What Blood Means for Us

Worth: “Incredible worth—God’s blood.” Counters voices (parents/society: “not worth much”). Prayer: Holy Spirit affirm.
Cleansing: Nothing too much—“What can wash my sin? Nothing but blood of Jesus.” Past/ongoing struggles.
Restoration: Beyond forgiveness—relationship w/o barriers. “Walk cleansed… covenant partners, reflect God to desperate world.”

Closing Reflection/Prayer
“Time of reflection… Sin brings death/rot, but God gave own blood for cleansing/restoration. You are worth it.” Prayer: See love, shed blood, life from death. Amen.

**LONG LIVE THE KING: Why Jesus Died and What It Means For Us All
**The Price of Freedom (Ransom)
**Main Scripture: Mark 10:32-45 NIV
**Jesus took the Twelve aside and told them what was going to happen to him. “We are going up to Jerusalem,” he said, “and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and the teachers of the law. They will condemn him to death and will hand him over to the Gentiles,  who will mock him and spit on him, flog him and kill him. Three days later he will rise.” Then James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came to him. “Teacher,” they said, “we want you to do for us whatever we ask.”  “What do you want me to do for you?” he asked. They replied, “Let one of us sit at your right and the other at your left in your glory.”
“You don’t know what you are asking,” Jesus said. “Can you drink the cup I drink or be baptized with the baptism I am baptized with?” “We can,” they answered. Jesus said to them, “You will drink the cup I drink and be baptized with the baptism I am baptized with,  but to sit at my right or left is not for me to grant. These places belong to those for whom they have been prepared.” When the ten heard about this, they became indignant with James and John. Jesus called them together and said, “You know that those who are regarded as rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their high officials exercise authority over them.  Not so with you. Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant,  and whoever wants to be first must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”
Additional Scripture: 

1 Corinthians 6:19-20
1 Timothy 2:5-6
Psalm 49:5-8

Quotes:
“The value of any commodity… is equal to the quantity of labor… Labor is alone the ultimate and real standard by which the value of all commodities can at all times and places be estimated and compared. It is their real price.”
- Adam Smith
“Christ gave Himself as a ransom for many, buying us from the hands of the devil by His own blood.”
- Origen
“God has not stood back and pulled levers. He has stepped into the situation himself, personally. That is in large part what the trope ransom means in the biblical literature. The principal idea is that of cost to God.”
- Fleming Rutledge
Outline
“Long Live the King – Ransom”
Sermon by Jay, Westgate Church
Text: Mark 10:32–45

I. Jay Introduces Himself and the Series Context


Greeting and personal introduction

“Good morning. Great to see you. If we’ve not met, I’m Jay, and I’m so grateful you’re here.”
Greets Saratoga room specifically; greets South Hills and Redwood City congregations and expresses joy in the shared journey as one church family.



Immediate move into teaching posture

States he wants to “jump right in” with a non‑rhetorical question and an image (a painting) to get everyone thinking.




II. Opening Question: What Is Something Worth?


Showing the first painting (Cézanne)

Displays a painting and asks people, very honestly, “How much would you pay for this?” encouraging blurting out answers (no hand‑raising, don’t overthink).
Hears answers like “a dollar,” “five dollars,” “twenty,” “a hundred,” and someone says “a million.”



Revelation of the painting’s actual value

Identifies the work as a painting by 19th‑century artist Paul Cézanne.
Says it sold at a Christie’s auction in November 2022 for $137 million, noting everyone would have “lost the bid.”



Additional paintings from the same auction

“Birch Forest” by Gustav Klimt – sold for $104 million that same night.
A Van Gogh painting – sold that night for $117 million.
In total, 60 paintings sold in one evening for $1.5 billion, the most money ever spent in a single art auction in recorded history.



Framing the main question

Asks rhetorically: What compels people to spend this kind of money on art?
Notes the discrepancy between initial audience estimates and the actual prices to expose how we think about value.




III. How Do We Determine Value?


Modern view: value as price someone will pay

Suggests that in the modern world, worth is often defined by the monetary price someone is willing to pay.
If someone pays 137M for the Cézanne, then “objectively” you can argue it’s worth 137M because that was the price actually paid.



Adam Smith and labor as value

Introduces Adam Smith, 18th‑century philosopher, “father of modern economics.”
Summarizes Smith’s idea: the value of a commodity is tied to the quantity of labor required to produce it; labor is the “real price.”



Illustration: Hilda’s family cookbook

Tells a story about an elderly couple, Chuck and Hilda, from a previous church.
At lunch in their home, Hilda pulls out a thick, dusty, tattered family cookbook, passed down over generations.
Pages show age at the front and become “newer” as later generations add recipes.
To an outsider, you wouldn’t pay much—maybe nothing—for the book, but to Hilda it is a priceless family heirloom she longs to pass on.
Point: its value is not the market price but the labor and love poured into it.



Illustration: friends’ newborn baby

Mentions several friends in the Westgate family who recently had babies, including a couple in his life group.
The journey to parenthood was long and hard; the baby massively disrupts their busy lives and costs them money.
The husband sends pictures of his exhausted face on the group text.
Yet he “cannot imagine life any other way” – the child is priceless despite the cost.
Point: true value is defined by the love and sacrifice invested, not monetary gain.




IV. Transition to Lent and the Cross: What Are We Worth to God?


Series frame: Long Live the King

States that in this Lenten season, the church is in a series “Long Live the King: Why Jesus died and what it means for us all.”
Notes they are exploring multiple biblical images that answer why Jesus died and what it means for us as they journey toward Good Friday and Easter.



Focus image for this sermon: ransom

Today’s focus is an image that highlights the immense cost and deep love expressed on the cross: the image of ransom.



Scripture: purchased at a price – 1 Corinthians 6:19–20

Quotes Paul: “You are not your own; you were bought at a price.”
Raises the question: If we were bought at a price, what was that price—a dollar, 5, 20, 100, 1M, $137M, or something else?



Scripture: Christ as ransom – 1 Timothy 2:5–6

Cites: “There is one God and one mediator between God and mankind, the man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself as a ransom for all people.”
Emphasizes that Jesus Himself—specifically His life given as ransom—is the price paid so that we might have life.



Our value before God

Whatever others say or we believe about ourselves, God determines our worth by the life of His Son offered for us.
To God, “you were worth His life.”




V. What Does “Ransom” Mean? Early Misunderstandings


Historical debate on ransom

Notes that the word “ransom” has been debated for centuries among Christian theologians.
In the early centuries of the church, many thought ransom meant God paying a price to Satan.



Origen’s view

Quotes early church father Origen, who said Christ “gave himself as a ransom for many, buying us from the hands of the devil by his own blood.”
Explains Origen held some heretical views, e.g., he did not believe in a literal, physical resurrection of Jesus, which undermines his reliability.



Rejection of ransom‑to‑Satan theory

States there is no biblical evidence that Satan has a legitimate ownership claim on human beings.
God does not pay Satan off; ransom is not a financial settlement with the devil.
This raises the key interpretive question: If the ransom is not paid to Satan, then what does the ransom imagery really mean?




VI. Exegesis of Mark 10:32–45 – The Ransom Saying in Context
A. Jesus Predicts His Passion – Mark 10:32–34


Third passion prediction

Jesus takes the Twelve aside and tells them what will happen in Jerusalem: He will be handed over, condemned to death, delivered to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, flogged, killed, and after three days, He will rise. Mark 10:32–34



The disciples’ self‑interested reaction

Immediately after Jesus speaks about suffering and death, James and John approach Him with a request.



B. The Ambitious Request – Mark 10:35–37


“Do for us whatever we ask”

James and John say, “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask,” which Jay calls a “ridiculous thing to say” to Jesus, yet notes how often we approach God similarly.



Desire for status and glory

Their request: “Let one of us sit at your right and the other at your left in your glory.” Mark 10:37
Jay explains ancient royal thrones: seats at the right and left of a king signified highest honor in the kingdom.



Contrast between Jesus’ mission and their expectations

While Jesus talks about suffering and a cross, the disciples are dreaming about status and a throne.
They assume Jesus came primarily to take power, but Jesus understands His mission as laying down power to make a crucial payment.



C. “Cup” and “Baptism” – Mark 10:38–40


Jesus’ response

“You don’t know what you are asking. Can you drink the cup I drink or be baptized with the baptism I am baptized with?” Mark 10:38
James and John confidently say, “We can.”



Future suffering of the disciples

Jesus replies they indeed will drink His cup and share His baptism, pointing to their future suffering and martyrdom for the faith after His resurrection.
He clarifies that seats at His right and left are not His to grant; they belong to those for whom they have been prepared. Mark 10:39–40



The other disciples’ indignation

The remaining ten become indignant with James and John. Mark 10:41
Jay infers their anger is not moral outrage but jealousy—they also want those seats and are upset that James and John asked first.



D. Redefining Greatness and Power – Mark 10:42–44


The Gentile model of leadership

Jesus gathers them and contrasts Gentile rulers who “lord it over” people and exercise top‑down authority. Mark 10:42



The kingdom model

“Not so with you.” Greatness in Jesus’ kingdom means becoming a servant, and being first means being slave of all. Mark 10:43–44
Jesus redefines power as self‑giving servanthood, not grasping for status.



E. The Ransom Statement – Mark 10:45


Jesus’ mission summarized

“For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” Mark 10:45



Meaning of “lutron” (ransom)

Notes the Greek word lutron always carries the idea of payment in the ancient world.
Three primary uses:

Payment to release slaves or captives.
Payment to rescue someone from execution.
Payment to absolve guilt of an offender.


So ransom implies payment for release or rescue.



What Jesus is saying about His death

When Jesus says He came to give His life as a ransom, He means He is paying the price for people’s release and rescue.
His death is a sacrificial payment so that we can be freed and forgiven, not a transaction with Satan.




VII. Old Testament Background: No One Can Pay for Life – Psalm 49:5–9


Reading from Psalm 49

Quotes the psalmist: those who trust in wealth cannot redeem the life of another or give God a ransom; “the ransom for a life is costly, no payment is ever enough.” Psalm 49:5–9



Meaning within Psalm 49’s context

The psalm’s point: no amount of wealth can save anyone from death.
You can pay off debt, but you cannot pay off death.



Illustration: Elon Musk and mortality

Uses Elon Musk as an example: richest person in history, yet he will still die like everyone else.
Confirms that human money cannot purchase escape from death.



The question that remains

If “no one can redeem the life of another” and “no payment is ever enough,” who can pay the price?




VIII. The Cross as God’s Costly Payment and Love


Jesus pays the price we cannot

Returns to Mark 10:45: Jesus gives His life as ransom, paying the price that we could never pay.
The price is not an amount of money but His own life and blood, given to defeat death and bring us life.



Fleming Rutledge’s insight

Quotes theologian Fleming Rutledge: God doesn’t stand far off pulling levers; He steps into the situation personally.
Ransom points to the cost to God—His own self‑giving love.



Payment not to Satan, but for our freedom

Clarifies again: Jesus’ “payment” is not a payoff to the devil.
The cross is God bearing the immense cost to free and unshackle us from what enslaves us: fear, pain, shame, bondage, guilt, and the consequences of sin.



The deadly seriousness of sin

The cross shows that sin is deadly and leads to death, which was never God’s original intent for humanity.
God is willing to pay the price of that death Himself so that we can have life.



Our worth before God

Our value is measured not in millions of dollars, but in the life of God’s Son, broken body and shed blood.
Jesus, a real person, died believing He was dying so that you might live.
Therefore, you are not an afterthought, not disposable, not too far gone, and not forgotten.




IX. Living as Those Who Are Ransomed and Free


The declaration of freedom

Repeats: “If you say yes to Jesus, you are free. The price has already been paid.”
Asks where we still live as though enslaved—hidden shame, secret struggles, addictions, or idolatrous goals that define our worth.



Identity secured

Asserts that who you are is already defined; your value and worth are already determined at the cross.
It was love that took Jesus to the cross, and He did it to set you free.



Call to respond in worship

Invites Chris and the worship team (and teams at other campuses) to come and lead in singing about God’s immense love.
Sends South Hills and Redwood City back to their pastors for a final movement of the teaching and response.




X. Auction Metaphor: Competing Bids for Your Soul


Returning to the art auction imagery

Re‑visits the Christie’s auction scene: a room with paddles raised as bids climb—10M, 50M, 100M, etc.
Describes how paddles go up and down until one remains at the final, highest price.



You as a work of art

Invites listeners to imagine themselves as a work of art being auctioned.
Many things are “bidding” for your soul:

The devil, as the enemy of God.
Your worries and fears.
Your anxieties, failures, flaws, insecurities.
Your circumstances, situations, unanswered prayers, unmet expectations, and unfulfilled ambitions.


Each of these bids to define you and enslave your soul.



The hand that outbids them all

Says the cross reveals one hand raised that will outbid them all.
It is the nail‑pierced, scarred hand of Jesus, not holding a paddle but bearing a wound of infinite worth.
As every other “bidder” tries to claim you, Jesus’ wounded hand stays raised saying, “No, you’re mine.”
He offers His life for your life, paying a price beyond compare.



You as priceless art

Affirms that you are a work of art beyond compare, loved in unfathomable ways.
Your worth is the highest price and greatest cost: the life of God’s Son, so that you might be called a child of God.



Scriptural echo: freedom in Christ – John 8:36

Cites: “Whoever the Son sets free is free indeed,” applying it to Jesus’ ransom work. John 8:36




XI. Closing Worship and Invitation


Song response: “Jesus Paid It All”

Leads the congregation into singing “Jesus Paid It All”, repeating lines like:

“Jesus paid it all, all to Him I owe.”
“Sin had left a crimson stain, He washed it white as snow.”


Uses the song to reinforce that Jesus has fully paid the debt of sin.



Final exhortation about the debt paid

Reiterates that Jesus paid not just any debt, but the ultimate debt owed to death so that we might live now and forever.



Prayer invitation

Invites the prayer team forward.
Extends a specific invitation to those exploring faith who realize they’ve never truly considered that death need not be the end of their story because of Jesus’ death and resurrection.
Also invites anyone carrying heavy burdens to come receive prayer.



Sending and benediction

Sends the congregation out to live in the confidence, courage, and comfort of knowing they are free and the debt of sin has been fully paid.
Encourages them to go in grace, peace, and love, reminding them again that the price is paid by Christ our Savior.

Condemnation (Satisfaction)
**Main Scripture: Colossians 2:13-15 NIV
“When you were dead in your sins and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made you alive with Christ. He forgave us all our sins, having canceled the charge of our legal indebtedness, which stood against us and condemned us; he has taken it away, nailing it to the cross. And having disarmed the powers and authorities, he made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross.”
Additional Scripture: 

Genesis 3:11–13
1 Timothy 4:1
2 Corinthians 5:10
John 9:39
Romans 2:5
Isaiah 3:13-15
Romans 8:1
Luke 9:52-55
James 3:9-10
John 3:17

Quotes:
_“In our present culture, “judgmental” has become one of the worst things that can be said about a person. We seem to have lost the ability to understand ‘judgment’ as having any positive connotation.”
_- Fleming Rutledge
“The wrath of God is always exercised in the service of God’s good purposes. It is the unconditional love of God manifested against anything that would frustrate or destroy the designs of his love.” 

Fleming Rutledge

“He was never opposed to us.  It is not his opposition to us but our opposition to him that had to be overcome, and the only way it could be overcome was from God’s side, by God’s initiaive, from inside human flesh—the human flesh of the Son.” 

Fleming Rutledge

Application:

Discerning God’s voice: Conviction vs Condemnation
Discerning God’s heart: Blessing vs Condemnation

Is there anyone in your life you’re condemning? 
Would you ask God to give you a heart of blessing?
Detailed Outline of Westgate Saratoga Sermon Transcript (March 8, 2026)
This outline closely follows the full transcript of the March 8, 2026 Westgate Church Saratoga gathering, with expanded bullet points and all illustrations. All verses that Pastor David or the service explicitly read are in bold and hyperlinked to Blue Letter Bible.

1. Welcome, Transition, and Worship Giving

The host welcomes everyone back and asks people to take their seats.
Announces that the gathering will continue with worship through giving.
Emphasizes:

Giving supports “the incredible ministry that is going on here at our church family.”
Most importantly, it supports “what God is doing through our local and global compassion partners.”
This is their best effort “to blur the lines between the church and our city and the world for Jesus’ name to be known all across the world.”


Practical giving instructions:

If prepared to give: scan the QR code.
Or drop off offering in the lobby on the way out.


Posture of heart for giving:

Invites the church to join in a written/prayed liturgical prayer:

Acknowledges that everything they have is from God.
Contrasts the world’s way (“spend all on ourselves and give without cost”) with the way of Christ (“sacrifice is the way of Christ”).
Asks God to help them steward resources so He might entrust them with true riches.
Prays for resistance to the delusion of riches and for growth in gratitude and generosity, “for your glory and for the good of the world.”




Concludes the giving section with “May it be so.”


2. Scripture Reading by Mike – Colossians 2:13–15

Transition: “As we prepare to hear today’s teaching, I’m gonna invite Mike up to read our scripture for today.”
Mike greets: “Good morning, West Gate Church.”
Mike thanks the congregation.
Main reading (explicitly read aloud):

Colossians 2:13–15
“When you were dead in your sins and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made you alive with Christ.
He forgave us all our sins,
having canceled the charge of our legal indebtedness, which stood against us and condemned us;
he has taken it away, nailing it to the cross.
And having disarmed the powers and authorities, he made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross.”


Mike concludes: “This is the word of the Lord.”


3. David’s Initial Response and Greeting

David responds humorously: “Mike, I think you should just preach… I’ll sit down. That was incredible. My goodness.”
Greets both in-person and Redwood City:

“Good morning. Also, Redwood City.”
Mentions first service streaming problem; Pastor Andrew in Redwood City had to preach immediately when stream stopped.
Hopes second service stream is working; if not, offers encouragement and prayer.


Introduces himself: “If we haven’t met, my name is David. I’m part of the team.”
Notes Daylight Savings:

“Happy Daylight Savings Day.”
Says there is “no judgment” if people came thinking it was first service.
Adds that if they fall asleep during his teaching, “again, no judgment, extra grace.”




4. Illustration #1 – Early Pastoral Ministry & “Nature Emergency”

Timeframe: “20 years ago” at the beginning of his pastoral ministry.
Role: Student ministries pastor; expresses deep love for working with youth.
Event:

Invited to speak to the adult congregation.
The night before, he had eaten a lot of Korean barbecue and drank lots of coffee (“what’s new in my life”).
He’s excited and prepared, worship team leads “typical” service flow, then it’s his time to preach.


Crisis:

As soon as he gets to the pulpit, “my stomach began to betray me badly.”
It “didn’t help that the passage I was reading was about Moses parting the Red Sea,” which adds humor to a gastrointestinal emergency.
He barely makes it through the scripture reading and knows he’s “done.”
Notes: “Seminary never trained me for navigating public speaking and nature emergencies.”


His response:

In haste, he decides to short-circuit the sermon.
Says something like: “Today, God just wants to speak through his word. You don’t need any pastoral explanation. The Bible alone is enough.”
Ends the sermon and leaves.


Later reflection:

Realizes he could have just said: “Hey church, my stomach is hurting and I need to just step aside.”
Instead, he confesses: “I lied.”
Motivation: He didn’t want to be judged or have people think less of him.
He “spiritualized” his fear using spiritual language.
Calls it “terrible, I know, terrible.”


Transition thought:

Connects this to fear of condemnation:

Fear of not being “good enough,” “impressive enough,” “spiritual enough.”
Says this fear of being exposed is not unique to him; “we are all afraid of being exposed.”






5. The Ancient Roots of Blame and Judgment – Genesis 3

Moves from personal story to Scripture: fear of exposure is ancient.
“This goes all the way back to the beginning”:

Humans decide to live apart from God.
God asks what happened in the famous Genesis story.


Reads/quotes:

Genesis 3:12
“The man said, ‘The woman you put here with me, she gave me some of the fruit from the tree, and I ate it.’”


Explanation:

The man takes no responsibility or ownership.
He blames the woman.
He also implicitly blames God (“the woman you put here with me”).


Continues narrative:

The Lord God asks the woman, “What is this you have done?”
The woman responds that the serpent deceived her; again, “not my problem.”


Point:

“Immediately after sin enters the world, blame enters the world.”


Quote from theologian Fleming Rutledge:

“We blame to get judgment off ourselves.”
David repeats it for effect: “Let me say that again, we blame to get judgment off ourselves.”


Observes:

Humanity has “a habit of dodging judgment.”


Clarifies difference:

Distinguishes between blame and judgment:

Blame condemns and retreats.
Judgment condemns and restores.


Says he’ll explain more on that later.




6. Our Preoccupation with Condemning Others

Notes that even if we’re not anxious about being judged, there is a universal trait:

“We are preoccupied with condemning someone else, whether that’s ourselves or others.”
Mentions canceling, blaming, eliminating people in our hearts.


Further Fleming Rutledge quote:

Cites her phrase, “whenever possible blame someone else.”
Says she “keenly points out the tension” in our present culture.


Cultural observation:

“Judgmental” has become one of the worst things to say about a person.
“Christians are judgmental” – a common charge.
We’ve “lost the ability to understand judgment as having any positive connotations.”


Problem statement:

Modern culture may resist the language of judgment.
But Scripture insists judgment is inescapable and necessary.




7. Scriptural Witness to Judgment and Wrath

David introduces several biblical examples of judgment:

1 Timothy 4:1 – Cited as: “In the presence of God in Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead.”
2 Corinthians 5:10 – “For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ.”
John 9:39 – “Jesus said, ‘For judgment I came into this world.’”
Romans 2:5 – “Because of your stubbornness and your unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath against yourself for the day of God’s wrath when his righteous judgment will be revealed.”


Emphasizes:

These texts show judgment and wrath are real and central themes.
This is only “a small sample among many.”


Acknowledges discomfort:

Says language of judgment and God’s wrath makes us “uncomfortable, confused, or afraid.”
Makes us want to “look away.”


Raises key questions:

“If God is loving and good, why does God judge?”
“How do we make sense of God’s wrath that’s in the Bible?”




8. Series Context – “Long Live the King” and Today’s Topic

Welcomes newcomers specifically: “If you are new, welcome to West Gate Church.”
Names current teaching series: “Long Live the King.”

Focused on journey toward Good Friday and Easter.
Exploring what Jesus did on the cross and what it means.


Today’s specific focus:

Imagery of God as judge.
How judgment connects to the cross, sacrifice, and God’s love.


Humor: Thanks Jay (another pastor/leader) for assigning “the easiest topics,” obviously sarcastic.


9. The Good News of God as Judge

Addresses the issue “head on”:

“God as judge is not bad news. It’s the best news.”


Reasons:

God is not indifferent to evil.
“A God who watches injustice and does nothing is not a good God.”
“A God who sees the oppressed and shrugs is not a God worth worshipping.”


Definition of God’s wrath:

“The wrath of God is not the rage of a tyrant.”
It is “the burning love of a Father who refuses to let evil have the last word.”


God’s judgment:

Is “the hope for a world full of injustice.”
Without judgment, there is no justice.
Without justice, evil and oppression go unanswered.


Fleming Rutledge quote on wrath:

“The wrath of God is always exercised in the service of God’s good purposes.”
“It is the unconditional love of God, manifested against anything that would frustrate or destroy the design of his love.”




10. Return to the Main Text – Colossians 2:13–15

David explicitly turns back to the central passage for the sermon:

Colossians 2:13–15 (re-read and paraphrased).


Explains imagery:

Paul paints a “courtroom scene.”
The cross is presented as a “courtroom event”:

There is a Judge.
There is a charge.
There is a verdict.
There is a real case against us.






11. Courtroom Imagery – The Case Against Us (Exhibits A–G)

David sets up a thought experiment:

“Think about this honestly: all the sins and evil we’ve committed.”
Warns he’s going to “depress us for the next two minutes,” but says “it will be okay.”


Uses courtroom language – “Exhibit A” through “Exhibit G”:

Exhibit A: “The ways we’ve wounded the people closest to us.”
Exhibit B: “The anger we’ve unleashed on our kids and the look on their faces after.”
Exhibit C:

“The lies we’ve told.”
Includes his own example of lying during teaching and preaching (the earlier story).
“The shortcuts we’ve taken.”
“The selfish decisions we’ve made.”


Exhibit D:

“The gossip and cutting words we’ve spoken to colleagues or friends or loved ones.”
Reminds that these are “words we can’t take back.”


Continues: “I’m not done, there’s another side… let’s keep going.”
Exhibit E:

“The times we’ve ignored the needs of the poor, the oppressed, or those who needed our help.”


Exhibit F:

“The envy, pride, and bitterness that have made their home in our hearts.”


Exhibit G:

“The countless moments we chose comfort over courage, fear over faithfulness.”
Even “the things that we carry from this week alone.”




Summary:

“All of it is just a lot.”
Collectively, it forms a heavy case against us and the burdens we carry.
Each person has their own list of misses, guilt, and shame.




12. The Good News – Jesus Bears the Judgment and Cancels the Debt

Pivot from guilt to grace:

“There is good news because we are not left to our guilt and shame.”
Jesus came “to take on that burden, to take on that judgment.”
Purpose: That we may have freedom and “life and life to the full.”


Connection to Easter:

This is why the church celebrates Easter.
Christ carries all that we were supposed to carry:

The sin, guilt, shame.
The hidden sins we keep from others.




Assurance:

Jesus does not leave us condemned.
He offers healing, forgiveness, love, and life.
“You are not known by your sin. You are known by God’s love.”


Restates main text emphasis:

The passage says Jesus “forgave us all our sins” (not some).




13. No Condemnation – Romans 8 and the Final Score Analogy

Explicit reference:

Romans 8:1 – “There is now no condemnation… for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Emphasizes:

Not “less condemnation.”
Not “delayed condemnation.”
“No condemnation.”




Legal verdict:

The verdict is not postponed or pending.
It has “been spoken in advance at the cross.”


Sports illustration:

David says he loves sports games.
Gives illustration:

A game played in the morning that you’re saving to watch later.
Someone blurts out the final score – very frustrating.


Yet there is something freeing about knowing the outcome:

You don’t “spiral over every turnover.”
You don’t panic over every mistake.
Because you already know the ending.




Spiritual parallel:

At the cross, God revealed the final score: “No condemnation.”
That’s “worth celebrating.”
Not just for those who “deserve it” or “have it all together.”
For those “who are in Christ Jesus,” who have said “yes” to Him.




14. Invitation to Say “Yes” to Jesus

David addresses those who have not yet responded:

The invitation is “freely given,” with nothing required except to say “yes” to:

His forgiveness.
His love.
His life.


Involves trading shame, guilt, burdens, and hidden things for His grace.


Encouragement:

“If you haven’t said yes, what an opportunity to say yes today.”


Practical step:

After the service, come to the table at the front.
The team would love to:

Talk.
Answer questions.
Walk alongside them.






15. For Those Who Have Said “Yes” – Justification and Transformation

Addresses believers:

Those who’ve already said yes to “this incredible love and forgiveness.”


Past misconception:

David used to think: “Sweet, I’ve been acquitted, case closed.”
But he notes: Forgiveness is only part of the story.


Key principle:

The gift declared over us (justification, no condemnation) is “unearned, freely given.”
That gift is meant to transform the way we move through the world.
“Right standing with God leads to right living.”


Pivot to practical issues:

Two main ongoing struggles for believers:

Judging ourselves.
Judging others.


Even though there is “no condemnation” in Christ, many still live as though condemned.




16. Practical Application #1 – Discerning God’s Voice: Conviction vs. Condemnation

David emphasizes:

This discernment is “one of the most important things you’ll ever learn” as a follower of Jesus.


He references a slide that compares conviction and condemnation:

Conviction from the Holy Spirit:

Very specific (identifies particular action or attitude).
Leads to hope of God’s transforming work.
Is relational and loving.
Invites and leads us to repentance (“that action was wrong, come back to Me”).
Names the sin but points to the Savior.
Encourages movement forward.


Condemnation from the critic (inner critic or enemy):

Vague and generalized.
Leads to shame and hopelessness.
Declares the person fully and totally defective.
Paralyzes (“you are wrong, you are hopeless”).
Names you as the problem and leaves you there.




Key contrast:

One restores identity (Spirit’s conviction).
The other attacks identity (condemnation).


Application:

We must discern: “Is that actually the voice of God?”
Or is it the voice of the enemy or our inner critic?




17. Practical Application #2 – Discerning God’s Heart: People of Blessing, Not Condemnation

David says:

God’s heart is to bless, not condemn.
Evidence: He would not have sent Jesus if He did not intend to bless the world.


Scriptural example – Disciples and Samaritans:

Luke 9:52–55 – Jesus sends messengers into a Samaritan village:

The people do not welcome Him because He is heading for Jerusalem.
Disciples James and John ask, “Lord, do you want us to call fire down from heaven and destroy them?”
Jesus turns and rebukes them.




Reflection:

David notes the extremity of the disciples’ reaction.
It’s easy to look at them as extreme and judgmental.
But this text is meant to be “a mirror” of our own souls, not a story to condemn the disciples.


Grocery line illustration:

David says he’s “not a big fan” of grocery lines at any store.
He values efficiency and speed (New York City and Silicon Valley background).
Scenario:

He’s in line, wants everything to move quickly.
The cashier is taking time, lovingly scanning every item, being kind to each vegetable.
Meanwhile, he’s internally praying for faster wrist movement.
To make it “worse,” the customer:

Engages the cashier in deep conversation.
Asks about struggles.
Offers to pray for them.


Irony:

They are “living into the life of Jesus” (caring, slowing down).
David admits he “hates it” in that moment because it slows him down.


Final “stage” that pushes him over the edge:

Payment moment – the customer hasn’t prepared their credit card in advance.
They start searching for it after everything is scanned, adding more delay.
David jokes:

He thinks you should have the card ready before you get in line.
Says, “Yes, if that’s you, I’m watching you. I’m judging.”








Point:

He admits his own judgmental reflex.
But reminds: “We’re called to be a people of blessing, not condemnation.”
The freedom and grace we have received (undeserved) should shape how we treat others.




18. The Tongue: Blessing God and Cursing People

David turns to another text about the tongue:

James 3:9–10 – “With it we bless our God and Father… and with it we curse people who are made in the image and likeness of God.”


Reflection:

Acknowledges this is unfortunately true in his own life.
Wants to “lean into the life of blessing towards others” more intentionally.


From John’s Gospel:

John 3:17 – “For God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through Him.”


Connection:

We have a real problem with pronouncing judgment on others.
But we bless others because:

God has cleared every charge against us.
He longs to do that same saving work in their lives.


Therefore, we are invited to move toward others with blessing, not condemnation.




19. Transition Toward Communion and Closing Story

David signals that he will invite the worship team up and move toward communion.
Notes that if streaming is working, Redwood City will be sent back to their campus pastor (Andrew).
Introduces a closing story to illustrate God’s heart further.


20. Illustration #2 – Financial Struggle and Father’s Provision

Context:

Early in David’s marriage, they experienced a season of serious financial struggle.
He acknowledges that some people in the room may be in that season “right now.”


Pastoral care note:

Emphasizes that financial difficulty is “really, really, really painful.”
Says he has a special heart for this because it has been part of his own story growing up.
Invites anyone struggling to come talk to the team.
Points to Care Pastor Mark (sitting in the room) as someone people can approach directly after the service for help.


Internal struggle:

Their situation becomes so bad that he needs to call his parents for help.
Wrestles for weeks:

What will his dad think?
Will he be disappointed?
Will he think David failed as a provider?


Embarrassment and shame build before he even makes the call.
He repeatedly pulls up his dad’s contact, then backs out (“not today”).


The call:

Eventually, it gets bad enough that he has to call.
He describes being awkward:

Asks his dad random questions: “How’s your life?” “How are your devotionals?”
His dad is confused: “What are you talking about?”
Finally, David gets honest:

“Dad, I don’t know how to say this, but I’m really struggling financially and I would love your help.”
He clarifies: He understands if his dad can’t help.
He apologizes, and admits he feels “embarrassed” to share this.






The father’s response:

Immediately: “Son, how much money do you need? I’ll send it over right away.”
Affirms: “Of course, you’re my son. Of course.”
Further reassurance:

“David, I know you’re older now, but you’re still my son. I got you.”
“Whatever you need, whatever struggles you have, you can call me.”
“If it’s within my responsibility, my power, my means, I would love to come alongside and help you and your family.”




David’s reflection:

As he tells this story, he says he misses his dad’s voice deeply.
Notes there was:

No lecture.
No shaming.
No judgment.
Only provision.


Acknowledges it cost his dad something (his own resources).
But says ultimately this story is about God’s heart, not just his earthly dad.




21. Connecting Story to God’s Heart

Application:

In that moment, David experienced something of God’s heart.
When we come to God in our need:

When we run out of resources, strength, excuses.
When we stop hiding that thing we don’t want anyone to know about.


God is not on the other end of the line waiting to condemn.
He is waiting to provide “over and over again.”


Summary image:

“That’s the kind of Father we have.”
The King who stands before us is the King who:

Was nailed to the cross.
Canceled all our debts. “All of it. All of it, friends.”






22. Communion Instructions

David transitions to communion as a church community:

Mentions elements are available in the back.
If someone didn’t receive the elements:

They can raise their hand and an usher will bring them.
Or they can go to the back and pick them up.




Explains the meaning:

The bread:

Represents the body of Christ “broken for us.”
Symbolizes Him taking “all of the judgment that we should have received.”
So that we might have “life and life to the full.”


The cup:

Represents the blood shed “for the forgiveness of not just some of our sins, but all of our sins, both past, present, and future.”






23. Guided Prayer Before Communion


David asks everyone to close their eyes and bow their heads.


Leads into two “prayer movements”:


First movement: Confession and Thanksgiving

Invites people to think about this week:

Ways they “missed the mark” with:

Loved ones.
Friends or co-workers.
Bosses.
Neighbors.
Spouses.
Children.




Reminds that Jesus offers forgiveness and healing.
Asks them to take a moment to thank Jesus:

That He does not leave them condemned.
That He offers life, grace, and forgiveness.





Second movement: People We Judge

Invites them to consider:

Is there anyone in their life they tend to condemn and judge quickly?
Is there a person the Holy Spirit is bringing to mind?


Clarifies:

The Spirit is not bringing this up to condemn or shame them, but to convict and invite change.


Encourages:

Pray for that person.
If not ready to bless them directly, pray: “God, would you help me be the kind of person who can bless?”
Or, if ready, simply speak a blessing over them in prayer: “Because of what you have done for me, I want to be the kind of person that offers your blessing.”








24. Taking the Communion Elements


After a time of silent prayer, David leads the church in taking the elements:


Bread

“This is the bread. This is the body of Christ on the cross, broken for us.”
Emphasizes:

Jesus takes on “all of the judgment that we should have received.”
So that “we might have life and life to the full.”


Invites them to take it “with gratitude in our hearts.”



Cup

“This is the blood shed for the forgiveness of not just some of our sins, but all of our sins, both past, present, and future.”
Invites them to take it together “with gratitude in our hearts.”






25. Closing Prayer and Call to Worship Response

David prays:

Acknowledges the world is “filled with judgment and condemnation.”
Asks that the church would be a people of blessing because:

God has blessed them “with heavenly riches” through the sacrifice of His Son.


Expresses gratitude:

“We are reminded once again of your great love.”
“We do not take your sacrifice for granted.”
Thanks Jesus for carrying what we cannot carry ourselves.
Emphasizes the burden is too heavy for us, and Jesus “literally died so that we may have life.”


Ends prayer in Jesus’ name, “Amen.”


Final instruction:

Invites everyone to stand.
Encourages them to respond in worship to His great love through song.

**Main Scripture: 1 Corinthians 15:51-57 NIV
“**Listen, I tell you a mystery: We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed—in a flash, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed. For the perishable must clothe itself with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality. Sermon Notes: Long Live the King - Why Jesus Died
Location: Westgate Church, Saratoga Campus
Speaker: Jay
Date: March 15, 2026
Series: Long Live the King: Why Jesus Died and What it Means for Us All

I. Opening: The Mystery of Transformation

Physical Condition: The speaker noted he was wearing a jacket despite it being 80 degrees outside and mentioned he was battling a lost voice, using tea and cough drops to power through.
Scripture Reading: 1 Corinthians 15:51-57.

We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed in the twinkling of an eye.
The perishable must clothe itself with the imperishable.
“Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?“.



II. Story: Nazi Fear Propaganda in Paris

The Poster: The speaker shared an image of a 1941 Nazi propaganda poster plastered in occupied Paris.
The Ultimatum: Following an assassination of a German soldier, the poster declared all detained French persons were now “hostages” and would be shot in response to further attacks.
The Goal of Propaganda: To squelch resistance through fear. The Nazis didn’t just hang posters; they conducted public hangings and firing squads to maintain control.
Historical Lineage: Empires from the Assyrians to the British have used the same message: “Resist and be crushed”.

III. The Roman Empire’s Propaganda: The Cross

The Instrument of Terror: For Rome, the cross was not just for execution; it was their favorite fear propaganda tactic.
Brutality by Design: It was designed to maximize humiliation and degrade the victim’s spirit.

Victims were stripped naked and beaten.
Strategic Placement: Crucifixions only happened on busy roads, outside city walls, or on hillsides (like Calvary) to elevate the symbol of power.


The Mechanics of Death: Victims died of slow suffocation. They had to pull their weight up by the nails in their wrists just to breathe.
Story: The Rebellion of Spartacus:

70 years before Christ, Spartacus led a slave revolt.
Upon his defeat, Rome took 6,000 rebel prisoners and crucified them along the 120-mile stretch of the Appian Way.
For days, anyone traveling that road saw thousands of bodies as a warning: “Rebel and this is your fate”.



IV. The Biblical Subversion of the Cross

Turning the Symbol: The New Testament writers flip the meaning of the cross from a symbol of Roman victory to a symbol of Christ’s victory.
Scripture: Colossians 2:13-15.

Jesus canceled our legal indebtedness by nailing it to the cross.
He “disarmed the powers and authorities” and made a “public spectacle of them,” triumphing over them.


Core Claim: Christ is not a victim of the cross; He is victorious through the cross.

V. The Unseen Realm and “Demonization”

Identifying the Enemy: Our struggle is not against flesh and blood (people), but against spiritual forces.
Scripture: Ephesians 6:12.
Story: The New York Pastor’s Insight:

Jay quoted a pastor who said: “When we cease to believe that there are demons, that’s when we begin to demonize people”.
Without a concept of a deeper malicious force, we blame our neighbors for all the world’s brokenness.


Invitation: Acknowledged the difficulty of believing in an “unseen realm” and invited skeptics to Alpha after Easter.

VI. The Victory Motif Throughout Scripture
The speaker highlighted that this victory isn’t a one-off event but the theme of the entire Bible:

Genesis 3:15: The offspring of the woman will “crush your head” (speaking to the enemy).
Isaiah 25:6-9: On this mountain, God will “swallow up death forever”.
1 John 3:8: The reason the Son of God appeared was to “destroy the devil’s work”.
Hebrews 2:14: By His death, He broke the power of him who holds the power of death.
Story: Backyard Basketball Trash Talk:

Jay shared a story of playing one-on-one with his son, Simon.
Simon started “talking trash,” so Jay used his height to palm the ball and keep it out of reach while boxing him out.
He used this to illustrate the taunting language of 1 Corinthians: “Where, O death, is your victory?” In Christ, we “have the ball” and the enemy cannot touch us.


Revelation 5:5: “The Lion of the tribe of Judah… has triumphed”.

VII. Personal Application: Facing Defeat

The “Already” Victory: The most important victory in history has already taken place.
Story: The Struggle of a Dad:

Jay shared that he has felt “deflated and defeated” over the last two weeks, specifically regarding his role as a father to his 10-year-old and 7-year-old.
He expressed the pain of realizing his own lack of skill or empathy has created unnecessary challenges for his kids.
He described “strongholds”—suffocating thoughts like “You’re a failure” or “You didn’t have a dad, and now your lack is playing out in them”.


The Solution: 2 Corinthians 10:4-5.

We have divine power to demolish these strongholds.
We take captive every thought and make it obedient to Christ.



VIII. Three Practices for the Week

Remember Divine Power: The power that raised Christ from the dead is literally available to you.
Call Out False Thoughts: If a thought isn’t from God, label it a lie.
Surrender Every Thought: Hand over the sense of defeat to the one who is already victorious.


Benediction Prayer: Jesus, come and defeat death again—the various deaths we face in our situations. Set us free and send us out unburdened and unafraid. Amen.

The Cross, Christus Victor, and Victory Over the Empire
Core theological theme
The sermon presents the cross through the lens of Christus Victor: Jesus’ crucifixion is not a defeat but God’s decisive victory over empires, unseen powers, sin, and death. The cross, originally a Roman tool of fear and control, is reinterpreted as God’s public proclamation of triumph over every power that enslaves humanity.

Fear propaganda, empires, and the cross


The sermon begins with a World War II Nazi leaflet posted in occupied Paris (August 22, 1941).

The notice states that:

All detained French persons will be regarded as hostages.
In the event of further attacks against German forces, a number of hostages “corresponding to the seriousness of the crime” will be shot.


This is identified as fear propaganda, designed to crush even the slightest thought of rebellion among occupied people.



The sermon notes that Nazis did more than hang posters:

They carried out public executions by hanging or firing squad across occupied territories (France, Poland, Czechoslovakia, etc.).



This tactic is placed in a long line of historical empires:

Assyrians, Persians, Egyptians, Mongols, Ottomans, Spanish, British, and even tongue‑in‑cheek references like the “Galactic Republic” and the Dodgers.
Across history, empires have leveraged fear propaganda to maintain power and suppress resistance.
The message is consistently: “Resist the empire and be crushed.”



The sermon locates Jesus’ death within this pattern:

At the time of Jesus, the Roman Empire ruled through military strength and technological advancement.
Rome’s primary form of fear propaganda was crucifixion—the cross.




Roman crucifixion as empire’s victory proclamation

The sermon quotes N. T. Wright to explain crucifixion:

Crucifixion was a central way for ancient authorities to show subject peoples “who was in charge” and to break any spirit of resistance.
It was “the sharpest and nastiest way” to assert absolute power and guarantee the victim’s absolute degradation.
It was not merely execution but deliberately designed for maximum humiliation.


Crucifixion logistics:

Victims were stripped naked and publicly displayed.
Crosses were placed:

On busy roads.
Just outside city walls.
On hills where everyone could see.


This placement mirrored how a modern business chooses high‑visibility spots for billboards; the cross was Rome’s billboard of terror.
Death by crucifixion came slowly by suffocation:

Victims had to push/pull themselves up to breathe.
Over time, exhaustion prevented them from lifting their bodies, and they suffocated.
The process could take hours or even days, ensuring prolonged public humiliation.





Spartacus and the Appian Way

A historical example illustrates crucifixion as political terror:

71 years before Christ, the slave revolt led by Spartacus was crushed.
In response, Rome crucified about 6,000 rebel prisoners along the Appian Way—a 120‑mile Roman road used by thousands daily.
Crosses were set up every short distance so that for 120 miles, travelers saw rebels slowly dying.
The message: “Resist the empire and die.”



Cicero on crucifixion

Cicero, a first‑century Roman philosopher, described crucifixion as:

“The most cruel and terrifying penalty.”
Something that should be far removed from a Roman citizen’s thoughts, eyes, and ears.
Even the mention of crucifixion was considered unworthy of a free Roman citizen.


Implication:

Crucifixion was reserved for rebels and non‑citizens.
It was a declaration against any thought or impulse of resisting the empire.
It functioned as a proclamation of victory over rebellion.




Reframing the cross: Colossians 2 and Christus Victor

The sermon then examines how the New Testament speaks of Jesus’ crucifixion, particularly in Colossians 2:13–15:

“He forgave us all our sins, having cancelled the charge of our legal indebtedness, which stood against us and condemned us; he has taken it away, nailing it to the cross. And having disarmed the powers and authorities, he made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross.”
Colossians 2:13–15 (Bible Gateway)


The sermon highlights:

The Roman cross was intended as a public spectacle of Rome’s power over rebels.
Paul claims that on that same cross, Jesus disarmed the powers and authorities and made them a public spectacle, triumphing over them.
The image shifts:

From Rome’s victory over a criminal.
To God’s victory over the very powers (seen and unseen) that claim to rule.




Central claim:

“Christ is not a victim of the cross; Christ is victorious through the cross.”


Roman soldiers’ reaction:

The Gospels record that after Jesus’ death—accompanied by an earthquake and darkened skies—battle‑hardened Roman soldiers, who had seen many crucifixions, said: “Surely this man was the Son of God.”
(Referencing Matthew 27:54, Mark 15:39, Luke 23:47.)
Matthew 27:54 (Bible Gateway)


The sermon stresses:

The cross, that ultimate symbol of imperial defeat, becomes the place of God’s victory proclamation.
Jesus’ work on the cross is portrayed as disarming and exposing the powers.




Unseen powers and authorities in the heavenly realms
The unseen realm (Ephesians 3 & 6)


The sermon explains that the “powers and authorities” in Colossians 2 are further described in Ephesians:

Paul speaks of “rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms” (Ephesians 3).
Ephesians 3:10 (Bible Gateway)
He also writes:

“Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this dark world, and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms.” (Ephesians 6:12).
Ephesians 6:12 (Bible Gateway)





The sermon notes:

There is an unseen, invisible world around, beneath, and all around the visible world.
This unseen realm influences events and experiences in our visible lives.
Even non‑Christians acknowledge unseen realities through concepts like quantum superposition and entanglement (multiple dimensions and unseen interactions), suggesting that “there is more than meets the eye.”



Christian belief:

Much (not all) of what causes injustice, pain, and brokenness is influenced by the malicious intent of unseen powers and authorities—the enemies of God.
These forces are larger than any single human villain (Hitler, Stalin, Pol Pot, etc.); they function like a puppeteer behind the scenes, seeking to enslave humans to selfishness, fear, and sin.



Balanced view of evil (C. S. Lewis)

C. S. Lewis is cited to encourage a balanced approach:

Christians should neither be naive about evil nor obsessed with it.
The goal is awareness of evil’s reality while keeping hope firmly centered on God.



Invitation to Alpha for skeptics

Recognizing that talk of invisible powers may feel “far out” or hard to believe, the sermon invites seekers to Alpha:

Alpha is described as a safe space to:

Have deep conversations about faith.
Ask questions that may be hard to voice elsewhere.
Journey alongside others exploring similar questions.




Whether or not one currently believes all this, the sermon asserts:

The cross claims that God is victorious over these unseen powers and authorities.
The cross is a victory over both visible and invisible enemies.




Victory motif from Genesis to Revelation
The sermon shows that the Christus Victor theme runs from the first book of the Bible to the last.
Genesis 3:15 – Head‑crushing promise

After the fall in Genesis 3, God speaks of enmity between the serpent and the woman, and between their offspring:

“He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.”
Genesis 3:15 (Bible Gateway)


The sermon interprets this as:

A prophetic word about Jesus, the ultimate offspring who will crush the head of Satan.
A clear declaration of future victory, not a tentative hope.



Isaiah 25:7–9 – Swallowing up death

Isaiah prophesies:

“On this mountain he will destroy the shroud that enfolds all peoples, the sheet that covers all nations; he will swallow up death forever. The Sovereign Lord will wipe away the tears from all faces…”
Isaiah 25:7–9 (Bible Gateway)


The sermon:

Connects “this mountain” to the hill where Jesus dies.
Emphasizes that God will swallow up death forever.
Notes the response: “Surely this is our God; we trusted in him, and he saved us… Let us rejoice and be glad in his salvation.”



1 John 3:8 – Destroying the devil’s work

1 John states:

“The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the devil’s work.”
1 John 3:8 (Bible Gateway)


This is presented as an explicit mission statement of Jesus: to destroy the works of the enemy.

Hebrews 2:14 – Breaking the power of death

Hebrews explains:

Jesus shared in humanity “so that by his death he might break the power of him who holds the power of death—that is, the devil.”
Hebrews 2:14 (Bible Gateway)


The sermon stresses:

Jesus becomes human in order to break the enemy’s grip on death through His own death.



1 Corinthians 15:54–57 – Death swallowed up in victory

1 Corinthians 15 declares:

“Death has been swallowed up in victory.
Where, O death, is your victory?
Where, O death, is your sting?…
But thanks be to God! He gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.”
1 Corinthians 15:54–57 (Bible Gateway)


The sermon notes:

This is taunting language toward death—mocking its supposed power.
Victory is not just Jesus’ but is given to believers in Christ.



Revelation 5:5 – The lion who has triumphed

Revelation gives a vision of the end:

“Do not weep! See, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed.”
Revelation 5:5 (Bible Gateway)


The sermon uses this to show:

The Bible begins with a promise of victory (Genesis 3) and ends with a vision of the Triumphant Lion, Jesus.




Where do you feel defeated? Fear propaganda in the soul


After tracing the victory motif, the sermon turns to personal application:

“Where do you feel defeated today?”
It acknowledges that many feel:

Family tensions.
Strained relationships.
Marital distance or pain.
Physical struggles (personal illness, caring for aging loved ones, difficult diagnoses).
Professional challenges (career insecurity, layoffs, changing industries, workplace frustration).
Internal struggles (restlessness, anxiety, depression, cynicism, lack of meaning and purpose).
Financial stress.
Hidden addictions or behaviors they cannot shake.





The sermon then reframes inner struggle in terms of fear propaganda:

The enemy of the soul (Satan and unseen powers) is likened to an empire dropping leaflets into the heart:

Messages of hopelessness (“It will never change.”).
Worthlessness (“You’re too broken; God could never use you.”).
“Not enough” (“You’ve done too much wrong; you’ve blown it.”).
Disappointment in God’s timing (“God isn’t coming through, so He must not care or act.”).





Key idea:

Following Christ does not guarantee a life without difficulty.
It does guarantee that God is with His people in the difficulty, and that the most decisive battle—the defeat of unseen powers—has already been won.
Victory over these powers means they have no lasting authority over those in Christ, and real freedom is possible.




Jesus’ own view of the cross: John 12


The sermon shows that Jesus Himself understood His death in victory terms:

“Now the prince of this world will be driven out. And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”
John explains that Jesus said this to show the kind of death He would die (crucifixion).
John 12:31–33 (Bible Gateway)



The sermon emphasizes:

Jesus saw His crucifixion as the moment when:

The “prince of this world” is driven out.
All people are drawn to Him by His lifted‑up death.


The cross is therefore Jesus’ chosen means of victory over sin, death, and the devil.



An invitation is extended:

Those who have never entered a relationship with Jesus are invited to come to the “I Said Yes” table after the service to ask questions and explore receiving this gift of victory.



The sermon underscores:

Jesus’ victory on the cross is truth—absolute truth.
The tension is that this truth does not always align with day‑to‑day emotional experience.




Fighting back when you feel defeated: 2 Corinthians 10
Divine power and taking thoughts captive

The sermon turns to 2 Corinthians 10:3–5 as a practical response:

Quotes:

Peter Scazzero, The Emotionally Healthy Leader

“Our society marshals enormous resources and ingenuity to make things happen. Immense stores of knowledge can be computerized and used in scientific enterprises that boggle the mind… But the very persons who are doing these things…the scientists who put men on the moon cannot get along with their own wives and children.”

Sermon Outline
The Cross, Substitution, and the True Elder Brother
The idea of substitution
It is a deeply human impulse to want someone else to take the blame or consequences we deserve. The Christian understanding of the cross centers on the idea that someone else actually did—Jesus willingly took our place and bore the consequences of our sin.
A key New Testament phrase is “hyper hemon” (Greek: for us), which Paul uses to describe what Christ did on the cross.

In Romans 5:7–8, Paul writes:

Very rarely will anyone die for a righteous person, though for a good person someone might possibly dare to die. But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.



This is the idea of substitution: Jesus willingly and sacrificially took our blame and our debt upon Himself.
A story to illustrate the cross
Jesus often explained the cross with a story rather than a lecture. In Luke 15:11–32, He tells the parable of two sons and a loving father.

The younger son demands his inheritance early (effectively saying, “I wish you were dead”), then spends everything in a distant country and ends up feeding pigs, destitute and ashamed.
When he “comes to his senses,” he decides to return home simply as a hired servant, but his father runs to meet him, embraces him, and throws a massive celebration.

However, the story turns on the older brother.

When he hears about the party for his younger brother, he becomes angry and refuses to go in.
Luke 15:28–30 describes his complaint:

The older brother became angry and refused to go in. So his father went out and pleaded with him. But he answered his father, “Look! All these years I’ve been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!”


The father had already divided the inheritance, giving the older brother two‑thirds. That means the celebration for the younger son actually costs the older brother; the robe, ring, feast, and music all come from his share.
The younger son’s welcome home is free for him, but not free overall—someone still has to absorb the cost.

This parable begins to show that the cross is not just our inspiration (“Jesus died to show us how to be nice”), but our rescue. Someone must pay the cost that we cannot.
The problem we cannot fix ourselves
Romans 7 describes a common human struggle:

Paul says, “I do not understand what I do. For what I want to do I do not do, but what I hate I do.”
This points to a power inside us—something the Bible calls sin—that is not just a list of bad actions, but a living force that shapes our patterns, impulses, and reactions and leads to death.

An author puts it this way: “Jesus may be in your heart, but grandpa is in your bones.”

There is a kind of spiritual DNA in us that pulls us away from who we want to be, no matter how hard we try.
The Bible describes humanity as enslaved to sin, trapped under death, and spiritually dead apart from Christ (see, for example, Romans 6; Hebrews 2; Ephesians 2).

Even in a culture that believes it can “innovate” its way out of anything, the truth is that we cannot rescue ourselves from this inner brokenness. We need a substitute.
The refusal to pay the cost
In the parable, the older brother is the one who should pay or accept the cost of restoration.

In first‑century Jewish culture, a good older brother would:

Pursue the younger brother.
Bring him home.
Accept the cost as part of his duty and honor.


Instead, this older brother stays home, resents the cost, and refuses to help.
Jesus ends the story with the brother still outside, the father pleading with him, and the question hanging in the air: If the older brother will not pay the cost, who will?

The tension is like a dinner party where no one has said who will pick up the tab. Everyone is watching; someone must pay. The question is left unanswered in the story—but the reader is pushed to ask: Where is the true elder brother who will willingly pay the cost?
Jesus as the true elder brother
New Testament writers point to Jesus as that true elder brother.


In Romans 8:29, Paul writes:

For those God foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters.
Romans 8:29 (Bible Gateway)



The writer of Hebrews says that Jesus is not ashamed to call them His brothers and sisters, and that He declares, “I will proclaim your name to my brothers and sisters; I will praise you among your assembled people.”


This means:

Jesus is the true elder brother who willingly pays the cost that we cannot.
He leaves everything to come looking for us, absorbs the cost to bring us home, and does not just forgive us in a mechanical transaction.
Instead, He calls us family and is not ashamed to call us brother or sister.

What really happened on the cross
The New Testament describes the cross as a real, historical event with real consequences:


1 Peter 2:24 says that Christ bore our sins in His body on the cross.
1 Peter 2:24 (Bible Gateway)


Galatians 3:13 says that Christ became a curse for us, redeeming us from the curse of the law.
Galatians 3:13 (Bible Gateway)


Romans 5 says that Christ died for the ungodly while we were still sinners, showing that God’s love comes to us before we have fixed ourselves.
Romans 5:7–8 (Bible Gateway)


And in Romans 8:31–32, Paul draws this conclusion:

If God is for us, who can be against us?
He who did not spare His own Son, but gave Him up for us all, how will He not also, along with Him, graciously give us all things?
Romans 8:31–32 (Bible Gateway)

The cross is therefore not a cold, mechanical transaction, but the heart of the Father giving the Son, and the Son willingly giving Himself, to bring us home.
An illustration of rescue
A child once disobeyed his father’s warning and climbed on a motorcycle, only to have it fall on him and pin him against a fence. The weight was crushing; he could barely breathe.

He was too afraid to cry out, terrified of getting in trouble.
When his father finally came, the child expected anger or frustration.
Instead, he saw love and concern; his father took the weight of the motorcycle onto himself, lifted it off his son, and brought him inside to the dinner table.

Theologically, this mirrors the cross:

Jesus steps under the weight of our sin, bearing what was crushing us.
He pays the cost that we could not, and brings us home to the table as family.

A call to invite others “Come home”
The story invites us to ask:

Who needs to hear, “Come home”?

Someone who feels too far from God.
Someone trapped under the weight of mistakes and shame.


The Bible says that the prayer of a righteous person is powerful and effective—not because we are perfect, but because we have been given Christ’s righteousness.

There is both a spiritual and practical response:

Pray for that person, naming them before God and asking Jesus to love and rescue them.
Then invite them concretely:

To an Easter service, or to come with you to church.
To sit at the table, hear the hope, and experience the grace that changes everything.



An invitation for you personally
If you feel the crushing weight of a self‑directed, sin‑filled life and are ready for forgiveness and rescue, the invitation is to come home today:

The Bible says that if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart, you are saved.
It also says that if you confess your sin, He is faithful to forgive.

The response is simple:

Come to the prayer team, say, “Today is my day,” and let them pray with you.
Even if it feels uncomfortable, this is how you step out from under the weight and into the embrace of the Father and the welcome of the true elder brother, Jesus.
