Teaching
**03-22-2026
LONG LIVE THE KING: Why Jesus Died and What It Means For Us All
**In Our Place (Substitution)
**Main Scripture: Romans 5:7-8 NIV
**“Very rarely will anyone die for a righteous person, though for a good person someone might possibly dare to die. But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Additional Scripture: 

Luke 15:11–32
Luke 15:28–30
Romans 7:15 
Romans 6:6–7
Hebrews 2:14–15
Ephesians 2:1–5
Romans 8:29
Hebrews 2:11-12 
1 Peter 2:24
Galatians 3:13
Romans 5:6–8
Romans 8:31–32

Quotes:
“Jesus may be in your heart… but Grandpa is in your bones.”

Peter Scazzero, The Emotionally Healthy Leader

“Our society marshals enormous resources and ingenuity to make things happen. Immense stores of knowledge can be computerized and used in scientific enterprises that boggle the mind… But the very persons who are doing these things…the scientists who put men on the moon cannot get along with their own wives and children.” 

Eugene Peterson, Five Smooth Stones for Pastoral Work

Closing Invitation:
Who needs to hear you say “Come home”?
Do you need to hear “Come home”?
Sermon Outline From Dave
The Cross, Substitution, and the True Elder Brother
The idea of substitution
It is a deeply human impulse to want someone else to absorb the consequence or debt that we owe. The Christian understanding of the cross centers on the truth that someone else actually did—Jesus willingly took the penalty for our sin and bore what we could not.
A key New Testament phrase is “hyper hemon” (Greek: for us), which expresses the idea of substitution: something being done on our behalf, in our place, for our sake.


In Romans 5:7–8, Paul writes:

Very rarely will anyone die for a righteous person, though perhaps for a good person someone might even dare to die. But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Romans 5:7–8 (Bible Gateway)



In 1 John 3:16, the idea appears again:

This is how we know what love is: Jesus Christ laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers and sisters.



In 1 Corinthians 15:3, Paul defines the gospel as:

For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures.



In John 10:11, Jesus says,

I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.



The pattern is clear: the cross is not merely a backdrop to ethics; it is a substitutionary event in which Jesus willingly, sacrificially took our place.


The story of the two sons and the father (Luke 15:11–32)
Jesus explains the cross not with a theological lecture, but with a story—a family story about two sons, a father, and a broken relationship.


In Luke 15:11–32, Jesus tells of a man with two sons. The younger son demands his inheritance early, effectively saying, “I wish you were dead so I can have your money now.”


The father gives him his share, the younger son leaves for a distant country, and squanders everything in reckless, “wild living,” becoming destitute and feeding pigs—a shockingly shameful state for a Jew.


When he comes to his senses (“rock bottom”), he plans to return home and say,

“Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants.”
Luke 15:11–32 (Bible Gateway)



But the father does not wait for the speech. When he sees his son coming from a distance, he runs to him, embraces him, restores his status with a robe and ring, and throws a great feast.


The older brother and the cost of the welcome
The story takes a sharp turn with the introduction of the older brother.

The older brother hears the music and learns that the party is for his younger brother, who has squandered the father’s property.
Luke 15:28–30 records his anger:

The older brother became angry and refused to go in. So his father went out and pleaded with him. But he answered his father, “Look! All these years I’ve been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!”


In the cultural setting, when the father divided the estate the older brother would receive two‑thirds and the younger one‑third. That means the celebration is paid for largely from the older brother’s share.
The younger son’s welcome home is free for him, but not free overall: someone still has to bear the cost. The older brother refuses to absorb that cost and therefore refuses to go in.

The cross is not just an example
The story shows that the cross is more than inspiration (“Jesus died to show us how loving we should be”); it is rescue.

The younger son represents anyone who has wandered far from God, morally bankrupt and spiritually destitute.
The father represents God, whose instinct is compassion and restoration, not rejection.
The older brother represents those who feel they have “earned” their place and are unwilling to let the cost be born on their behalf—or to extend grace to others.
The real problem is not just distance from God, but the truth that we cannot repair ourselves. The Bible describes humanity as enslaved to sin, trapped under death, and spiritually dead apart from Christ (see, for example, Romans 6; Hebrews 2; Ephesians 2).

The older brother’s refusal and the unanswered question
Jesus leaves the story unresolved:

The older brother stands outside, the father is pleading with him, and the question hangs in the air: If the older brother will not pay the cost, who will?
The older brother does not just refuse out of pride; there is also an underlying inability. The New Testament often speaks of sin as a debt so great that we cannot pay it.
The implication is that even if the older brother wanted to, he could not cover the cost that the younger brother owes. The debt is insurmountable.

Jesus as the true elder brother
In this light, New Testament writers point to Jesus as the one who actually plays the role of the true elder brother.


In Romans 8:29, Paul writes:

For those God foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters.
Romans 8:29 (Bible Gateway)



In Hebrews 2:11–13, the author says:

Both the one who makes people holy and those who are made holy are of the same family. So Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers and sisters. He says, “I will declare your name to my brothers and sisters; in the assembly I will sing your praises.”
Hebrews 2:11–13 (Bible Gateway)



These passages reveal that:

Jesus is the true elder brother who willingly bears the cost that we could not.
He is not ashamed to call us brothers and sisters.
He leaves everything to come looking for us, absorbs the debt, and brings us home.

What happened on the cross
Across the New Testament, the cross is described as a historical, substitutionary event:

Christ bore our sins in His body on the cross (1 Peter 2:24).
Christ became a curse for us, redeeming us from the curse of the law (Galatians 3:13).
Christ died for the ungodly while we were still sinners (Romans 5:6–8). Romans 5:7–8 (Bible Gateway)
John 3:16 captures the motive behind it all:

For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life.
John 3:16 (Bible Gateway)



Paul also draws the logical conclusion in Romans 8:31–32:

If God is for us, who can be against us?
He who did not spare His own Son, but gave Him up for us all, will He not also graciously give us all things?
Romans 8:31–32 (Bible Gateway)

Substitution is therefore a real transaction—a real payment that we could not make—but it is motivated by love, with the purpose of bringing us home.
The call to “come home”
The story and the New Testament together point to a simple but profound invitation: Come home.

The older brother had the opportunity to join the party, to share in the celebration, but he stayed outside because of resentment and refusal to absorb the cost.
The father represents God saying, “Everything I have is yours. We had to celebrate because this son was lost and is now found.”
The true elder brother, Jesus, steps in not only to pay the cost, but to invite others in:

Those who feel far from God.
Those who feel trapped under shame and brokenness.
Those who think they have gone too far to be welcome.



Implicit in the text is both a personal response and a missional response:

Personally, you are invited to come home to the Father, not based on your performance, but on the substitutionary work of the true elder brother.
Relationally, you are invited to extend the same invitation to others: to pray for them, to speak words of “come home,” and to invite them into the celebration of grace.

The shape of a life under substitution
A life that understands substitution looks like this:

It knows that salvation is not self‑achievement; it is rescue.
It is marked by gratitude, not pride, because the cost was paid by another.
It is willing, like the true elder brother, to bear cost for others, to help bring the “lost” home.
It worships the Father who sent the Son and the Son who willingly gave Himself, knowing that if substitution is true, then God’s heart toward us is radically different from what we fear it to be.

In short, substitution is not a cold, mechanical transaction; it is the Father’s love, expressed through the Son’s obedience, bringing prodigal sons and resentful older brothers alike into the same family, at the same table, with the same invitation: Come home.

Teaching
**03-29-2026
LONG LIVE THE KING: Why Jesus Died and What It Means For Us All
**Re-Storied (Recapitulation)
Main Scripture: Romans 5:19-21 NIV
“Just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous. The law was brought in so that the trespass might increase. But where sin increased, grace increased all the more, so that, just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness to bring eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”Additional Scripture: 

Genesis 3:6-10 
Psalm 51:5 
Psalm 58:3 
Romans 8:22 
Matthew 27:50-51
John 1:14
Philippians 2:7
2 Corinthians 3:18
Colossians 1:19-20
1 Corinthians 15:21-22 
Romans 6:4 

Quotes:
_“In the primal event, ‘Adam’ was disobedient… rebellion against the good purpose of God. Because of that catastrophic primordial event of disobedience, the whole consequent history of humankind has been a saga of estrangement and folly. […] Redemption, therefore, involves a radical reconstituting of human nature… not on human possibility and potential, but on the power of God… The story of Adam and Christ is a story of incapacity on the part of Adam and potency on the part of God.”
_-Fleming Rutledge
“[Though] the Witch knew the Deep Magic, there is a magic deeper still which she did not know. Her knowledge goes back only to the dawn of time. But if she could have looked a little further back, into the stillness and the darkness before time dawned, she would have read there a different incantation. She would have known that when a willing victim who has committed no treachery was killed in a traitor’s stead, the table would crack and death itself would start working backwards_.”
_-The Lion, The Witch, and The Wardrobe” by C.S. Lewis (1950)
The Cross, Rupture and Repair, and God Rewriting Our Stories
Core theological theme
The sermon presents the cross as God’s decisive repair of humanity’s deep rupture with Him, rewriting stories of loss, guilt, shame, and death into stories of attachment, healing, and new life. This is framed through the pattern of “rupture and repair” in human psychology and Scripture, showing that in Jesus’ death and resurrection God enters our rupture, bears its cost, and opens the way for comprehensive reconciliation and transformation.

Rupture, loss, and the human story

The sermon begins with well‑known Disney and Pixar films (e.g., Frozen, Up, The Lion King, Finding Nemo, Moana, Cinderella, Snow White, Tarzan), observing that a central common theme is loss, specifically the death of a loved one.
In many of these films, the death occurs:

On screen during the story.
Or before the story begins, casting a long shadow over the plot.


The film Up is used as an example: its opening montage presents a short, emotionally powerful story of love and devastating loss, illustrating how deeply such stories can move viewers.

Walt Disney’s personal story of loss

A historical story about Walt Disney is told:

In 1938, after the success of his early work, Walt Disney purchased a beautiful home in North Hollywood for his parents, Elias and Flora, as a 50th wedding anniversary gift.
Later that year, on November 26, 1938 (two days after Thanksgiving), a gas leak in that home killed his mother, Flora.


This sudden tragedy left a deep mark on Walt Disney:

He carried significant guilt for the rest of his life, feeling responsible because he had provided the home.
The loss of his mother shaped his internal world as a son and as a human being, not just as a filmmaker.


Psychologists who have studied Disney storytelling note that repeated themes of parental loss in his stories tap into something profoundly effective and resonant in human hearts.
This personal tragedy strangely contributed to immense professional success, because stories built around the loss of a loved one connect deeply with the human experience.


Rupture and repair in psychology and life

The sermon names a key psychological dynamic that underlies such storytelling: rupture and repair.
In psychological terms:

Rupture describes moments when relationships break or seem to be breaking—experiences of separation, abandonment, loss, or betrayal.
Repair describes the restoration of those relationships—when safety, trust, and attachment are re‑established and strengthened.


Human beings are born with a deep drive to attach to others in a healthy way:

Christian psychologist Curt Thompson is quoted: “We are all born into the world looking for someone looking for us.”
Healthy attachment to God, to others, and even to ourselves is built through cycles of rupture and genuine repair.



Personal story: first day of school


A personal story is told about the first day of elementary school:

As a six‑year‑old, the child had been primarily cared for by an aunt while the mother worked.
One day, without fully understanding what was happening, the child was taken to an unfamiliar school, surrounded by strangers and a language not yet understood.



The experience:

Felt like rupture—a sense of abandonment and betrayal (“They are going to leave me here forever”).
Captured the fear many children feel when suddenly separated from their primary caregiver.



At the end of that first day, however, the mother returned:

The second day was still scary, but less so, because there was now a memory that the mother came back.
By the third day, there was a growing expectation that the mother would return again.



Principle illustrated:

Rupture without repair leaves a person broken, insecure, and unable to form healthy attachments.
Rupture followed by consistent repair builds deeper trust and stronger attachment, leaving an enduring mark on a person’s relational life.



The sermon uses this to explain:

Rupture is unavoidable in a fallen world; everyone experiences relational breaks.
True repair, when it happens, builds capacity for secure, trusting relationships and becomes the foundation for healthy attachments, including attachment to God.




The biblical story: the first rupture in Genesis 3

To understand the cross as repair, the sermon returns to the beginning of the biblical story, showing that a major relational rupture lies at the heart of humanity’s story.

The Genesis 3 narrative


The sermon reads from Genesis 3:

The woman sees that the fruit of the tree is good for food, pleasing to the eye, and desirable for gaining wisdom, so she takes some and eats it.
She also gives some to her husband, who is with her, and he eats it.
Their eyes are opened; they realize they are naked; they sew fig leaves together and make coverings for themselves.
They hear the sound of the Lord God walking in the garden in the cool of the day and hide among the trees.
The Lord calls, “Where are you?” and the man replies that he was afraid because he was naked, so he hid.



This passage is Genesis 3:6–10.
Genesis 3:6–10 (Bible Gateway)


The sermon then summarizes:

God, a good God, creates a beautiful garden that represents all of creation.
God creates human beings, male and female, to tend the garden and steward creation.
Everything is good, beautiful, and true; God dwells among humans in a loving relationship with nothing between them.



The enemy of God appears as a serpent and deceives the humans regarding the one tree God had forbidden them to eat from.


The humans disobey, rebel against God, and the relationship between God and people is ruptured:

They hide.
They feel fear, shame, and distance.
The intimacy they once enjoyed is now fractured.



Born into rupture

From Genesis 3 onward, Scripture portrays all people as born into this state of rupture.
Psalm 51 is quoted:

“Surely I was sinful at birth, sinful from the time my mother conceived me.”
Psalm 51:5 (Bible Gateway)


Psalm 58 is also quoted:

“Even from birth the wicked go astray; from the womb they are wayward.”
Psalm 58:3 (Bible Gateway)


These texts show that:

Every human being comes into a world already marked by sin and brokenness.
There is a deep, inherited condition of rupture that colors every aspect of human life.



Creation’s groaning

The sermon then notes that it is not only people but the entire creation that is affected:

Paul writes in Romans 8: “We know that the whole creation has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth right up to the present time.”
Romans 8:22 (Bible Gateway)


The world itself groans under disorder, decay, and death—evidence that the original rupture has cosmic consequences.


The cross as the means and moment of repair

The sermon states a central conviction:

The cross of Jesus—where Jesus dies and gives His life so that others might have life—is both the means and the moment by which God repairs the problem of rupture and rewrites the entire story.



Fleming Rutledge on rupture and redemption

Theologian Fleming Rutledge is quoted, describing Genesis 3 as “the primal event”:

In that event, Adam (or the first humans) was disobedient, rebelling against the good purpose of God.
Because of this catastrophic, primordial disobedience, human history has become a saga of estrangement (rupture) and folly.


Rutledge explains that redemption involves a radical reconstituting—a remaking—of human nature:

Not built on human possibility and potential.
But grounded in the power of God.


This highlights:

Human beings are incapable of repairing the deepest rupture through their own strength.
Only divine power can truly heal the break between God and humanity.



Human potential vs. God’s power

The sermon contrasts:

The cultural obsession with human possibility and potential—especially in regions like Silicon Valley, where technology and wealth lead some to imagine transcending human limits and even achieving a form of immortality.
The biblical conviction that sin and death lie beyond the reach of human ingenuity and cannot be overcome by human power alone.


The story of Adam and Christ is described as:

A story of incapacity on the human side.
A story of potency and power on God’s side.


All the varied ruptures people experience—guilt, shame, fear, regret—are rooted in that first rupture, which introduced sin, brokenness, and death into the human story.


Personal rupture and the need for repair


The sermon applies the idea of rupture personally, asking:

Do you have any guilt, shame, fear, or regret in your life right now?
Do you feel distant from God, from someone you love, or even from yourself?



Examples are given:

A decision you made (or failed to make) that you wish you could redo.
A relationship you broke but do not know how to fix.
A deep, dark, hidden thing you never want anyone to discover—an action, event, thought, or feeling from your past.
The persistent sense that you should be further along in life, leading to a belief that you are not enough and never will be.



The sermon notes that:

Many followers of Jesus find it easier to believe, in general, that “God forgives sins” than to believe God forgives that particular sin or that particular wound they most want to hide.
Understanding that all these personal ruptures are rooted in the first rupture of Genesis 3 can be strangely relieving:

It does not excuse sin or remove responsibility.
But it clarifies that people are born into a world already fractured, and this deepest fracture cannot be repaired by human effort.





Hope arises from the truth that repair is possible—not because humans are powerful, but because God is powerful:

Despite human incapacity, God’s potency is fully expressed on the cross.




Romans 5: the rewriting of Adam’s story


The sermon returns to Romans 5, which was read earlier:

“Just as through the disobedience of the one man, the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man, the many will be made righteous.
The law was brought in so that the trespass might increase. But where sin increased, grace increased all the more, so that, just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness to bring eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”



This passage is Romans 5:19–21.
Romans 5:19–21 (Bible Gateway)


Key points drawn out:

Adam’s disobedience made the many sinners; Jesus’ obedience makes the many righteous (put right with God).
Righteousness is something people are made, not something they make themselves; it is a gift rooted in God’s power, not human potential.
Where sin increases, grace increases all the more—God’s grace is heavier, stronger, and larger than any weight of guilt or shame.
Grace now reigns through righteousness to bring eternal life through Jesus Christ.



Application:

When the weight of guilt, shame, fear, and regret feels overwhelming and suggests a particular rupture cannot be repaired, Scripture insists that God’s grace is still greater.
No matter how heavy sin feels, grace is heavier still.




The curtain torn: a new rupture that heals the old


The sermon notes that the original rupture (Genesis 3) is repaired at the cross by a different kind of rupture:

“When Jesus had cried out again in a loud voice, he gave up his spirit. At that moment the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom.”



This is Matthew 27:50–51.
Matthew 27:50–51 (Bible Gateway)


The temple context is explained:

The temple was the center of Jewish religious life, the place people believed they had to go to meet with God.
Within the temple, the Holy of Holies was the most sacred inner space, considered God’s space—the place where heaven and earth met.
Only the high priest could enter the Holy of Holies, and only once a year, after careful ritual purification; entering wrongly meant death.
A thick curtain separated God’s space from human space, symbolizing that God was hidden from sinful humanity.



This curtain is linked back to Genesis 3:

When sin entered the story, humans hid from God; later the curtain symbolized that same separation—humans and God hidden from each other.



At Jesus’ death:

The curtain is “torn in two from top to bottom”—a rupture initiated by God, not by humans.
This physical tearing signifies that the barrier between God and people has been removed.



The theological meaning:

When Jesus dies on the cross, the story of rupture is repaired and rewritten.
Death is “killed,” the grave is put “six feet under,” so that a new story of access, closeness, and life with God becomes possible.




Three ways the story is rewritten by the cross
The sermon identifies three key dimensions of how the cross rewrites the human story.
1. Incarnationally – the story is rewritten “in the flesh”

The story is first rewritten incarnationally, meaning that God does not heal the rupture from a distance but by coming in the flesh in Jesus.
John 1:14 is cited:

“The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us.”
John 1:14 (Bible Gateway)


Philippians 2 is also referenced:

Jesus “made himself nothing by taking the very nature of a servant, being made in human likeness.”
Philippians 2:7 (Bible Gateway)


Implications:

Jesus fully empathizes with human pain: the heaviness of guilt, shame, fear, and regret is known from the inside.
God is not detached or dismissive; God understands, shares, and bears human suffering.



2. Transformationally – the story is rewritten by changing us

The story is also rewritten transformationally:

Jesus does not just sympathize with pain; He transforms it.


2 Corinthians 3:18 is cited:

“We all, who with unveiled faces contemplate the Lord’s glory, are being transformed into his image with ever‑increasing glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit.”
2 Corinthians 3:18 (Bible Gateway)


This means:

Those who turn to Christ are in a continual process of being reshaped into His likeness.
Jesus enters the space of pain, shame, guilt, and regret not only to comfort but to redeem, restore, and re‑author the story.



3. Comprehensively – the story is rewritten for all things

Finally, the story is rewritten comprehensively:

It is not just about individual lives; God is rewriting the story of the whole world.


Colossians 1:19–20 is quoted:

“For God was pleased to have all his fullness dwell in him, and through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether things on earth or things in heaven, by making peace through his blood, shed on the cross.”
Colossians 1:19–20 (Bible Gateway)


This means:

Jesus will ultimately heal and reconcile all things—everything broken by sin, including wars, injustice, and inequity.
The cross is not only personal but cosmic; it sets in motion the final renewal of creation.




Palm Sunday: Jesus reversing the direction of exile

The sermon connects Palm Sunday to the theme of story‑reversal and repair:

Palm Sunday remembers Jesus’ entry into Jerusalem during Passover in the days leading up to His arrest, crucifixion, and resurrection.


In the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John), Jesus is greeted as a triumphant king:

People wave palm branches, a symbol of Jewish victory.
They celebrate and applaud His arrival, treating Him as a victorious ruler.



East of Eden and Jesus’ route

The sermon then revisits Genesis 3 after the fall, when God banishes humans from the garden:

The humans are sent “east of Eden.”
This refers to Genesis 3:23–24.
Genesis 3:23–24 (Bible Gateway)


The direction is significant:

Eastward exile symbolizes being sent out of God’s presence because of sin.


Some Gospel accounts describe the geography of Jesus’ approach to Jerusalem (e.g., from Bethphage and the Mount of Olives).
See, for example, Matthew 21:1–11.
Matthew 21:1–11 (Bible Gateway)
When these locations are mapped, Jesus is seen to enter Jerusalem from the east.
The symbolism:

Humanity was banished eastward, away from God’s presence.
Jesus, moving westward into Jerusalem from the east, is pictured as reversing that exile—coming in to repair the rupture and rewrite the story.
As He enters, He is greeted with branches and leaves (palms), evoking the imagery of a garden and hinting at the restoration of what was lost.




Death and resurrection: Adam and Christ


The sermon then quotes Paul:

“For since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead comes also through a man. For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive.”



This is 1 Corinthians 15:21–22.
1 Corinthians 15:21–22 (Bible Gateway)


Paul further explains in Romans 6:

“We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may live a new life.”



This is Romans 6:4.
Romans 6:4 (Bible Gateway)


The theological logic:

Death entered through Adam; resurrection comes through Christ.
In Adam, all die; in Christ, all who belong to Him are made alive.
Baptism symbolizes being buried with Christ and raised to a new kind of life, even now.




Baptism as an enacted picture of the rewritten story


The sermon invites those who have not been baptized to consider baptism on Easter weekend:

Baptism is described as a physical, embodied, symbolic, sacramental reminder that God, through Christ’s death and resurrection, wants to rewrite a person’s story.



Practical invitations:

Opportunities to be baptized at upcoming Good Friday and Easter gatherings are announced.
People are encouraged to sign up (via QR codes or welcome tables) if they are followers of Jesus who have not yet been baptized.



Baptism is portrayed as:

Public identification with Christ’s death and resurrection.
A visible declaration that the old story of rupture is being left behind, and a new story of life with God is beginning.




Joining God’s work in others’ stories

The sermon also calls listeners to participate in God’s rewriting work in others:

Reference is made to a previous teaching that invited people to identify three individuals whose stories need to be rewritten by God’s grace.


Practical step:

Prayer cards are made available so people can write down the names of three individuals and pray for them throughout the week.


Encouragement:

Listeners are urged to invite one or two of those people to Easter gatherings, trusting that God’s Spirit may encounter them there.
The hope is that these friends will see that God can rewrite their stories, repair what is broken, and allow life to begin again in the midst of fear, guilt, shame, and regret.




The deeper magic: C. S. Lewis and death working backward
The Narnia story: Aslan and the witch

The sermon turns to C. S. Lewis’s The Chronicles of Narnia, particularly The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, which retells the Christian story in fictional form.
In the story:

Aslan the lion represents Jesus.
The witch represents the great enemy of God—Satan, the devil.


A crucial scene is described:

Aslan gives his life on a stone table for a wrong committed by someone else (a traitor).
The witch kills Aslan, believing she has won.
Yet Aslan later comes back to life, astonishing the children who have befriended him.



The “deep magic” and the “deeper magic still”


The children ask Aslan how he could be alive after they saw him die.


Aslan explains:

“Though the Witch knew the Deep Magic, there is a magic deeper still which she did not know. Her knowledge goes back only to the dawn of time, but if she could have looked a little further back, into the stillness and the darkness before Time dawned, she would have read there a different incantation. She would have known that when a willing victim who has committed no treachery was killed in a traitor’s stead, the Table would crack and Death itself would start working backward.”



The sermon uses this quote to draw out a key principle:

The “deep magic” is like the moral order of the universe:

Sin really does have consequences.
Justice demands that treachery be punished.


The “deeper magic still” represents something even more fundamental:

The eternal character of God, whose deepest nature is self‑giving love.
When an innocent, willing victim dies in the place of a guilty traitor, the power of death is broken and begins to work in reverse.





Applied to the cross:

Jesus, the sinless, willing victim, dies in the place of sinners.
At the cross, the deepest reality of the universe is revealed: God’s love is more foundational than sin or death.
Because of this, “death itself starts working backwards,” and what has been ruptured can be repaired.




Invitation to personal response


The sermon closes with a pastoral invitation:

Listeners are asked to close their eyes and ponder whatever feels ruptured in their lives:

A painful situation or circumstance.
A broken relationship.
Internal turmoil or darkness.


They are invited to quietly ask God, by His Spirit:

To repair the rupture.
To rewrite their story.
To help them live a brand new story through the death and resurrection of His Son.





The core invitation is to trust that:

Through Jesus’ cross and resurrection, God is actively rewriting stories of rupture into stories of repair.
Guilt, shame, fear, regret, and pain are not the final word; in Christ, death itself has begun to work backward, and new life is possible.

LONG LIVE THE KING: Why Jesus Died and What It Means For Us All
**Re-Storied (Recapitulation)
Main Scripture: Romans 5:19-21 NIV
“Just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous. The law was brought in so that the trespass might increase. But where sin increased, grace increased all the more, so that, just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness to bring eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”Additional Scripture: 

Genesis 3:6-10 
Psalm 51:5 
Psalm 58:3 
Romans 8:22 
Matthew 27:50-51
John 1:14
Philippians 2:7
2 Corinthians 3:18
Colossians 1:19-20
1 Corinthians 15:21-22 
Romans 6:4 

Quotes:
_“In the primal event, ‘Adam’ was disobedient… rebellion against the good purpose of God. Because of that catastrophic primordial event of disobedience, the whole consequent history of humankind has been a saga of estrangement and folly. […] Redemption, therefore, involves a radical reconstituting of human nature… not on human possibility and potential, but on the power of God… The story of Adam and Christ is a story of incapacity on the part of Adam and potency on the part of God.”
_-Fleming Rutledge
“[Though] the Witch knew the Deep Magic, there is a magic deeper still which she did not know. Her knowledge goes back only to the dawn of time. But if she could have looked a little further back, into the stillness and the darkness before time dawned, she would have read there a different incantation. She would have known that when a willing victim who has committed no treachery was killed in a traitor’s stead, the table would crack and death itself would start working backwards_.”
_-The Lion, The Witch, and The Wardrobe” by C.S. Lewis (1950)
The Cross, Rupture and Repair, and God Rewriting Our Stories
Core theological theme
The sermon presents the cross as God’s decisive act of rewriting the human story of rupture, sin, and death into a story of repair, reconciliation, and new creation. This is framed through the theological idea of recapitulation: in Jesus, God re‑runs and rewrites the human story from the inside, healing the primordial rupture of Genesis 3 and every subsequent rupture in human lives and in all creation.

Rupture and repair in our stories


Many beloved Disney and Pixar films (such as “Finding Nemo,” “The Lion King,” “Bambi,” etc.) begin with the tragic loss of a loved one, often a parent, especially a mother.


This recurring pattern is traced historically to Walt Disney’s own story: after the success of Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937), he bought a house for his parents as a gift, but in 1938 an undetected gas leak in that home killed his mother, Flora Disney.


The loss of his mother left an indelible mark on Disney’s life, and stories of parental loss and personal tragedy began to show up repeatedly in Disney films.


These stories of tragedy strangely resonate with filmgoers everywhere and even contribute to Disney’s professional success, because they mirror the deep patterns of human experience.


Psychologists describe a relational pattern called “rupture and repair.”

Rupture: a relationship is torn or broken by separation, abandonment, loss, or betrayal.
Repair: the relationship is restored so that safety, trust, and attachment are renewed and even strengthened.



Rupture without repair leaves people broken, insecure, and unable to attach in healthy ways, drifting emotionally and relationally.


When rupture is actually healed through real repair, relational bonds can become deeper and stronger, and people grow in wholeness.


This dynamic of rupture and repair is present not only in Disney storytelling but also in every human life and relationship.


The sermon situates Easter and the cross within this pattern: the cross is described as the climactic act of God’s repair in the face of the deepest rupture.


The series title, “Long Live the King: Why Jesus Died and What It Means for Us,” frames this sermon’s focus on how Jesus’ death rewrites the story of rupture into a story of restoration.



Recapitulation: God rewriting the story

The sermon introduces the theological term recapitulation to describe God’s work of rewriting human stories and the story of the whole world.
This idea is traced back to Irenaeus, an early church father (c. 130–202 AD), who taught that God is in the business of rewriting human stories, not only individually but cosmically.
Recapitulation means that in Christ, God enters the human story, re‑lives it correctly, and redirects its outcome toward restoration and life.


The first rupture: Genesis 3


The sermon goes back to the beginning of the biblical story to show the first and foundational rupture: humanity’s rebellion against God in the Garden of Eden.


God creates the Garden of Eden, representing all creation, and places humans there to tend it, steward creation, and walk with God in faithful covenant partnership.


God’s intention is intimate relationship: for humans to be His people and for Him to be their God, with nothing between them.


In Genesis 3, humanity chooses rebellion:

The woman sees that the fruit of the tree is good for food, pleasing to the eye, and desirable for gaining wisdom; she takes and eats and gives some to her husband, who also eats.
Their eyes are opened; they realize they are naked; they sew fig leaves together and make coverings for themselves.
They hear the sound of the Lord God walking in the garden in the cool of the day and hide among the trees; God calls, “Where are you?” and the man responds that he was afraid because he was naked, so he hid.



This passage is identified as Genesis 3:6–10.
Genesis 3:6–10 (Bible Gateway)


This scene shows the first relational rupture:

Distance now exists between humankind and God.
Fear, shame, hiding, and blame enter the relationship.



From this point on, all humanity is born into this rupture. Things are not as they should be.


Psalm 51 is cited to describe this condition: “Surely I was sinful at birth, sinful from the time my mother conceived me.”
Psalm 51:5 (Bible Gateway)

The sermon clarifies that this does not mean babies are committing conscious wrongs, but that every person is born into a broken reality that shapes every aspect of personhood.



Psalm 58 is cited to go further: “Even from birth the wicked go astray; from the womb they are wayward.”
Psalm 58:3 (Bible Gateway)

This emphasizes that human life begins within an already fractured world and a bent condition.



Paul is quoted in Romans 8:22: “We know that the whole creation has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth right up to the present time.”
Romans 8:22 (Bible Gateway)

The sermon highlights that not only humans but the entire creation is groaning under the weight of rupture and longing for repair.



Every form of brokenness, fear, and shame is traced back to this primal rupture in Genesis 3:

Sin, selfishness, violence, and death enter the world through this event.
All human shame, fear, regret, and longing for repair flow from this foundational break between God and humanity.




Human attempts at repair and their limits


Humans instinctively recognize that something is wrong and try to fix it.


Human beings, made in the image of God, possess real power and potential, and this leads to the belief—especially in places of innovation like Silicon Valley—that any problem can be solved.


However, even in regions of tremendous technological and economic power, deep relational and moral brokenness remain:

Marriages fail.
Parents and children become estranged.
Individuals and communities still experience deep pain and need.



The sermon stresses that the core problem—sin and rupture with God—cannot be solved by human intelligence, creativity, or effort.


The power needed for true repair is not found in human capacity but in God’s power and willingness to heal, especially through the cross.



The cross as the decisive repair

The sermon teaches that the cross of Jesus is the means and the moment through which God begins to repair the problem of rupture and rewrite the human story.
Fleming Rutledge’s work on the crucifixion is quoted to frame this:

In the primal event, Adam’s disobedience brought catastrophic estrangement and folly upon human history.
Redemption involves a radical reconstituting of human nature, not based on human potential but on the power of God.


The story of Adam and Christ is described as:

Incapacity, weakness, and rebellion on Adam’s side.
Power, potency, and saving initiative on God’s side in Christ.


All the various ruptures in personal lives are rooted in that singular rupture in Genesis 3.
The cross addresses not just individual guilt but the cosmic condition of brokenness, sin, and death.


Romans 5 and the reversal of Adam’s story


The sermon turns to Paul’s explanation of the cross as the rewriting of Adam’s story:

“Just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous.”
“The law was brought in so that the trespass might increase. But where sin increased, grace increased all the more, so that, just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness to bring eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”



This text is identified as Romans 5:19–21.
Romans 5:19–21 (Bible Gateway)


The sermon emphasizes:

Adam’s disobedience made many sinners; Christ’s obedience makes many righteous—right with God.
Sin’s growth only highlights the superabounding nature of grace.
Grace now “reigns” through righteousness, bringing eternal life through Jesus Christ.



When Jesus died on the cross, the original rupture was repaired; the central barrier between God and humanity was decisively addressed.



The temple curtain and the end of separation


The sermon recalls the Old Testament temple system:

God desired to dwell with His people, so the temple became the place of His presence.
People brought sacrifices at the temple to know with certainty that they were forgiven and could enter renewed relationship with God.
The temple layout moved from outer courts to inner courts to the “Holy of Holies,” the innermost space where God’s presence was said to dwell above the ark of the covenant—His throne.



A massive, richly colored curtain (blue‑purple, embroidered with gold and Edenic imagery) separated the Holy of Holies from the rest of the temple, symbolizing the separation of God’s space from human space.


The sermon then cites Matthew’s account of Jesus’ death:

“When Jesus had cried out again in a loud voice, he gave up his spirit. At that moment the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom.”



This passage is Matthew 27:50–51.
Matthew 27:50–51 (Bible Gateway)


The detail “from top to bottom” is highlighted:

If it had been torn from bottom to top, one might attribute it to human action.
Torn from top to bottom signifies God Himself has torn the curtain and removed the separation.



The theological point:

There is now no separation between God and humanity for those in Christ.
People no longer need to go to a specific sacred building to meet God; God rushes out to meet people anywhere and everywhere.
Any place can become a meeting place with God when a person calls on Him—and sometimes even when they do not, as God can surprise people with His presence.



This event marks the beginning of God’s great rewriting of the story, turning a narrative of distance and exclusion into a narrative of access and nearness.



How God rewrites the story: three core truths
The sermon identifies three core ways God rewrites the human story through the cross.
1. The story is rewritten in person (incarnation)


God does not rewrite the story from a distance; God comes personally into the story in Jesus.


The theological term is incarnation: God the Son takes on human flesh and lives as a human being in our world.


John’s Gospel is cited: “The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us.”
This is John 1:14.
John 1:14 (Bible Gateway)


Philippians 2:7 is also referenced: Jesus “made himself nothing” (emptied Himself), taking the very nature of a servant and being made in human likeness.
Philippians 2:7 (Bible Gateway)

This “emptying” means Christ set aside the privileges of His divine status in order to enter fully into human life and suffering.



The sermon stresses:

God does not remain aloof from human suffering; in Christ, God enters it.
Jesus does not merely understand suffering conceptually; He empathizes with it because He has experienced it.



A New Testament teaching is alluded to: believers do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with their weaknesses; instead, Jesus understands what they are going through. (Hebrews 4:15)
Hebrews 4:15 (Bible Gateway)


A pastoral analogy is used:

Superman would be useless to Metropolis if he did not have powers, but he would also be ineffective if he never left the Fortress of Solitude.
Similarly, God is both powerful and present; He has come near and remains involved.



The key pastoral assurances:

God is here—present with His people in their pain.
God is powerful—able to act and save.
Both are true at the same time, and this is very good news.



2. The story is rewritten to change us


God’s purpose is not only to change external circumstances but to transform people from the inside out.


The sermon notes that often what is broken is not just the situation but the person: hearts, minds, character, and desires.


Paul’s words in 2 Corinthians are cited:

“And we all, who with unveiled faces contemplate the Lord’s glory, are being transformed into his image with ever‑increasing glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit.”



This is 2 Corinthians 3:18.
2 Corinthians 3:18 (Bible Gateway)


God is actively working by His Spirit to transform believers into the image of Christ:

Changing how they think.
Changing how they respond to pain.
Rewriting their identity and character over time.



The sermon applies this deeply:

Pain, shame, guilt, fear, regret, and even the sense of “never being enough” are not the final word on a believer’s life.
Jesus wants to transform these experiences and their hold on a person’s story.



A psalm is referenced where the psalmist says he was trapped in a pit full of mud or “quicksand,” unable to get out, and God lifted him out and set his feet on a firm foundation.
This echoes Psalm 40:1–3.
Psalm 40:1–3 (Bible Gateway)


Jesus later teaches not to build on sand but on a firm foundation—Himself.
This reflects Matthew 7:24–27.
Matthew 7:24–27 (Bible Gateway)


Together these images show:

Jesus pulls people out of unstable, destructive places and sets them on the solid rock of Himself.
God’s rewriting of the story includes deep, internal change, not mere external fixes.



3. The story is rewritten completely (comprehensively)


The sermon insists that there is no aspect of a person’s story that is beyond God’s ability to enter and rewrite.


There is no brokenness too deep, no situation too frightening or overwhelming that God cannot address.


Paul’s language in Colossians is cited:

God was pleased to have all His fullness dwell in Christ and through Him to reconcile to Himself all things, whether things on earth or things in heaven, by making peace through His blood, shed on the cross.



This is Colossians 1:19–20.
Colossians 1:19–20 (Bible Gateway)


This means:

Nothing lies outside the scope of Jesus’ reconciling work.
Every kind of brokenness can be touched and transformed by Christ.



The sermon states that Jesus heals and reconciles “everything,” and that He is actively rewriting every story to the depths.


A pastoral picture is offered:

Some brokenness feels like a coffee cup with a small chip—annoying but not catastrophic.
Other times, life feels like that cup shattered into a thousand pieces—seemingly beyond repair.



The sermon suggests that God may be “best” at putting broken things back together and making them more beautiful than before:

The testimony of countless believers through history is that God has restored them from places of severe shattering.
God rebuilds lives in ways beyond what people can imagine.




Death, resurrection, and new life in Christ


Paul’s teaching in 1 Corinthians 15 is cited:

“Since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead comes also through a man. For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive.”



This is 1 Corinthians 15:21–22.
1 Corinthians 15:21–22 (Bible Gateway)


The sermon emphasizes:

In Adam, humanity inherits death.
In Christ, people are made alive—this is the heart of the rewritten story.



Romans 6:4 is then referenced:

“We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may live a new life.”
Romans 6:4 (Bible Gateway)



Key points drawn from this:

Believers are united with Christ in His death and resurrection.
New life is not only a future reality (eternal life after death) but a present reality now; God begins rewriting the story in the present.




Baptism as a visible sign of the rewritten story


The sermon describes upcoming baptisms on Easter Sunday:

A large tank of water will be placed at the front, and people from diverse backgrounds who have come to Christ will be baptized.



Though their stories differ, one thing is common: Jesus is writing a new story in each of their lives and bringing them out of spiritual death into life.


Baptism is portrayed as:

A visible sign of being buried with Christ and raised to new life.
A public celebration of God’s rewriting work.



Listeners who have already been baptized are invited to remember:

What Christ has done for them.
What their lives might have been like had Christ not intervened.



The hope is that this remembrance stirs worship and compassion, motivating believers to invite others who feel hopeless and believe their stories can never change.



The deeper magic: C.S. Lewis and substitutionary love
The Edmund story in The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe


The sermon closes with a story from C. S. Lewis’s The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe.


In the story:

Edmund, in his brokenness, betrays his siblings.
He later realizes in horror that his treachery has real consequences.



The White Witch invokes the “deep magic” written at the dawn of time:

The blood of every traitor belongs to her.
Edmund’s life is forfeit; she has the right to kill him.



This “deep magic” represents the moral order of the universe:

Sin has consequences.
Treachery demands death.
Wrongdoing must be punished.



Everyone lives under this reality; it is not a bureaucratic technicality but woven into the fabric of existence.


The White Witch is portrayed as a legalist who knows the rules and insists they be enforced—and she is “right” in that Edmund truly did betray his family.


Aslan’s substitution and the deeper magic


Aslan, however, knows a “deeper magic” the witch does not understand.


In a private conversation, Aslan offers to trade his own life for Edmund’s.


Aslan willingly walks into the witch’s camp:

He endures insults, humiliation, shaving, binding, and finally death on the Stone Table at the hands of the witch and her minions.



Lewis explains:

If the witch had looked further back, beyond the dawn of time into the stillness before time began, she would have read a different incantation:

When a willing victim who has committed no treachery is killed in a traitor’s stead, the Stone Table will crack, and death itself will start working backward.





The sermon’s theological point in retelling this:

There is something deeper and more powerful than sin and brokenness.
At the core of reality is the very character of God, whose essence is love.
Love is the highest ethic and truest foundation; the logic of divine love is that God Himself becomes a willing, innocent, substitutionary sacrifice for traitors.



This “deeper magic” in Lewis parallels the gospel:

Justice is real; sin truly has consequences.
But beneath justice lies the deeper foundation of God’s love, by which God willingly absorbs the full weight of justice on behalf of sinners.




Justice, love, and the cross

The sermon weaves together:

The reality of moral law (justice, consequences for sin).
The deeper reality of God’s character (love, self‑giving, substitution).


The cross is presented as:

The place where God, in Christ, willingly takes the punishment that justice rightly demands.
The act by which God “writes a new story” for humanity and creation.


Therefore:

Death is not the end.
Sin is not the end.
Tragedy is not the end.
Brokenness is not the end.


The resurrection and the cross together proclaim that God’s restorative love has the final word.


Pastoral application: living into the rewritten story


The sermon addresses common struggles:

Guilt over past decisions.
Shame and fear.
Broken relationships (including those personally damaged by one’s own actions).
Lingering regret and a sense of never being enough.



All of these are traced back to the original rupture of sin entering the world, but the cross proclaims that repair is now possible.


The call is to:

Bring all forms of rupture—personal, relational, internal—to God.
Trust that God is actively rewriting stories through Christ’s death and resurrection.
Participate in this “re‑storying” by surrendering to God’s mercy and walking with Him into new life.



The sermon prays that:

God would remind listeners that He is in the business of rewriting stories.
God would put the world—and individual lives—back together for His glory and for the good of people.



The final hope held out is that God is presently, actively rewriting the stories of everyone who turns to Him, and that His love in Christ is the deepest reality underneath every rupture.
